item.title: Anaplan
item.description:
Anaplan lets large organizations plan in a connected way. Instead of separate spreadsheets for finance, sales, and operations, teams build models on a shared platform so a change in one area, such as a drop in demand, flows through to inventory, headcount, and budget. Its modeling engine handles large multidimensional data, and planners can create scenarios to see the effects of different decisions before committing.

AI features aim to lower the barrier to building and using models. An assistant can help create or modify model logic from natural language, forecast with machine learning, and summarize results for decision-makers. The platform integrates with ERP, CRM, and data warehouse systems to pull in actuals, and offers applications for common planning needs, such as sales territory planning and supply chain optimization.

item.title: AVEVA
item.description:
AVEVA serves heavy industry with software for designing and running plants. Engineering tools support the design of facilities such as refineries and power stations in 3D, process simulation helps engineers model how plants will behave, and operations software monitors and controls equipment in real time. The PI System, which it acquired through OSIsoft, collects and stores time-series data from industrial sensors across thousands of sites.

AI and analytics sit on top of this data. Predictive analytics monitor equipment for early signs of failure, and optimization tools help reduce energy use and improve throughput. Industrial AI assistants help operators and engineers search documents and data, and digital twin capabilities connect engineering models with live operations. The company’s AVEVA Connect cloud platform brings these tools together.

item.title: BigQuery
item.description: BigQuery lets teams analyze huge amounts of data without managing servers. You load data from files, databases, streams, or other Google services, write SQL, and BigQuery spreads the work across many machines and returns results quickly, whether the table holds millions or trillions of rows. Because storage and compute are separated and managed, there is no cluster to size or tune, which is a big reason analytics teams like it.

item.title: Bloomberg Terminal
item.description: The Bloomberg Terminal is the main workstation for traders, portfolio managers, analysts, and bankers. It delivers real-time and historical prices across stocks, bonds, currencies, and commodities, together with news, research, company data, and analytics. A command-based interface lets users call up functions with short codes, which is why people who use it daily rarely touch menus. Its messaging system, Bloomberg Chat, is also where much of the market does its dealing.

item.title: BrightEdge
item.description:
BrightEdge targets big websites where SEO is a team effort. Its platform tracks rankings across many keywords and markets, ties organic traffic to revenue, and shows which pages are doing well. Content recommendations point to topics worth writing about and pages to improve, using data on search demand and competitor performance.

AI plays two roles. Inside the platform, machine learning finds patterns and generates recommendations. Outside it, the company tracks how brands appear in AI-generated search results and answer engines, a newer measurement area for marketers. Reporting suits agencies and enterprise teams that must show results to executives.

item.title: BuzzSumo
item.description:
BuzzSumo helps content marketers learn what already works. You enter a topic or domain and see the pieces that earned the most engagement on social networks, along with backlinks, so you can see what resonates before writing. Filters narrow by date, format, and language, which makes it easy to find trending ideas.

Other features cover outreach and monitoring. The influencer search finds people who regularly share and write about a topic, alerts notify you when a keyword or competitor is mentioned, and question tools show what people ask about a subject. AI helps generate ideas and outlines from the findings, and reports can be exported for clients.

item.title: Deepnote
item.description:
Deepnote reimagines the Jupyter notebook for teams. Several people can edit a notebook at once, comment on cells, and run code on managed cloud machines without setup. It connects to data sources such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Postgres, and supports SQL blocks alongside Python, so analysts can mix queries and analysis.

Results are easy to share. Notebooks can be published as interactive apps or dashboards with inputs, charts can be built without code, and scheduled runs keep outputs fresh. Version history and permissions help with team workflows, and it works with common libraries and Jupyter files.

item.title: Elasticsearch
item.description: Elasticsearch stores documents as JSON and indexes them so searches come back in milliseconds, even across billions of records. It began as a full-text search engine for things like product catalogs and website search, and it is also used heavily for logs, metrics, and security data. It is the core of the Elastic Stack, which adds Kibana for dashboards, and ingestion tools for getting data in. Companies use it wherever they need to search or aggregate a large volume of text-heavy data quickly.

item.title: FactSet
item.description:
FactSet is one of the main data providers for banks, asset managers, and hedge funds. It aggregates information from many sources into a single platform: company financials, earnings estimates, ownership, supply chain relationships, news, transcripts, and market prices. Analysts use it to screen companies, build models, check ownership, and prepare reports, and portfolio managers use its analytics to measure risk and performance.

Delivery options range from the FactSet Workstation, an interface with analytics and charting, to data feeds and APIs that supply data to a firm’s own systems, and add-ins for Excel. Generative AI features let users search and summarize documents such as earnings calls and filings in natural language, and the company offers tools to connect its data to AI applications and agents. It also provides content for wealth managers and corporate users.

item.title: FamilySearch
item.description:
FamilySearch lets anyone explore their family history without paying. Users search a vast collection of historical records, including census, birth, marriage, death, immigration, and military records, from many countries, and many are digitized images. A collaborative family tree combines contributions from millions of people, so you can often find relatives and connect with branches others have researched.

Technology plays a large role in making records searchable. Handwriting recognition and machine learning transcribe and index scanned documents at scale, which has opened up collections that would take volunteers years to index by hand. Tools suggest possible record matches for people in your tree, and photo and story features preserve family memories. The service also operates local centers and online help.

item.title: Firebase
item.description:
Firebase lets developers build apps without running their own servers. Its core services are Cloud Firestore and Realtime Database for storing and syncing data, Authentication for sign-in with email, phone, or social accounts, Cloud Storage for files, Hosting for websites, and Cloud Functions for server-side code. Analytics, Crashlytics, and Cloud Messaging for push notifications round out the app lifecycle tools, and SDKs support iOS, Android, web, Flutter, and Unity.

AI has become part of the platform. Gemini in Firebase helps developers write code, debug, and understand their projects, and Firebase AI Logic gives apps a secure way to call Gemini and other models directly from the client. Genkit is an open-source framework for building AI features and agents, and Firebase Studio provides a browser-based environment for prototyping apps with AI assistance.

item.title: FullStory
item.description:
FullStory lets teams see how real people use their websites and apps. It captures sessions, which can be replayed like a video of the user’s screen, and detects signals such as rage clicks, dead clicks, and error clicks that suggest frustration. Searching across sessions helps teams find all users affected by a particular bug or those who abandoned a checkout step, instead of guessing from numbers alone.

Beyond replays, it offers analytics such as funnels, heatmaps, and journey maps, and tools for tying issues to revenue impact. AI features summarize sessions and surface patterns, so teams don’t have to watch hundreds of recordings, and help prioritize the problems that matter most. Privacy controls mask sensitive information, and integrations send findings to engineering and support tools like Jira and Slack.

item.title: FutureHouse
item.description:
FutureHouse works on automating scientific research. The lab builds language-model agents that read and reason over the research literature, and makes some available to scientists on a platform. Crow answers questions with cited sources from papers, Falcon performs deeper literature reviews, and Owl helps check whether a topic has been studied.

A more ambitious project, Robin, links agents into a multi-step workflow. Agents suggest hypotheses, plan experiments, and analyze results, and the lab used the system to propose a candidate treatment, which was then tested experimentally. The goal is to speed up discovery by letting agents handle parts of the loop.

item.title: Grafana
item.description: Grafana is the dashboard tool many engineering teams reach for first. It connects to data sources such as Prometheus, Loki, Elasticsearch, PostgreSQL, and cloud monitoring services, and lets you build panels and dashboards that visualize time-series data, with alerts that notify teams when something goes wrong. Because it does not store data itself, it can sit on top of whatever you already collect, which is a major reason it is so widely adopted.

item.title: Heap
item.description:
Heap approaches analytics with automatic capture. Once its snippet is on a site or app, it records user interactions without developers adding tracking code for each event. Product managers can then define what counts as a signup or a purchase later and look back at historical data, which avoids the gaps that come from forgetting to instrument something.

Analysis tools include funnels, retention, user paths, and session replay, and a feature that surfaces friction points and drop-offs. It supports building segments of users and comparing their behavior, and it can send data to a warehouse. Heap was acquired by Contentsquare, which combines its quantitative analytics with Contentsquare’s digital experience tools.

item.title: ImageTrend
item.description:
ImageTrend makes software for first responders. Paramedics and EMTs record patient information, treatments, and outcomes on a tablet or computer, producing the report used for handoff to hospitals, billing, and quality review. The data also feeds state and national registries.

The company also provides tools for state EMS offices, trauma and stroke registries, and hospital data collection, as well as analytics for system performance. Newer tools use AI to help reduce documentation time and check data quality.

item.title: IQVIA
item.description:
IQVIA sits at the center of the pharmaceutical industry’s information flow. It collects and sells data on prescriptions, healthcare utilization, and patient activity from a large number of sources, which companies use to understand markets, size opportunities, and plan commercial strategy. The company is also a major contract research organization that runs clinical trials, recruiting patients, managing sites, and handling data on behalf of drug developers.

Technology and AI are applied to both lines of business. Analytics platforms combine data sets to deliver insights to sales and marketing teams, and AI helps identify suitable trial sites and patients, predict enrollment, and automate documentation and safety reporting. IQVIA has been building AI agents for tasks such as data analysis and trial operations, often in partnership with large technology companies.

item.title: Kaggle
item.description:
Kaggle is where many data scientists learn and prove their skills. Companies and researchers post competitions with real problems, such as predicting outcomes from data or classifying images, and participants submit models to a leaderboard. Winning solutions are often published, and the discussion forums are a rich source of techniques. Rankings and medals help build a public track record.

The platform offers more than contests. Public datasets cover topics from health to sports, free notebooks run Python and R in the browser with access to GPUs and TPUs within limits, and a models hub shares pretrained models. Kaggle Learn provides short, practical courses on Python, pandas, machine learning, and more. Benchmarks and community challenges around large language models have been added, and the site integrates with Google Cloud.

item.title: Maltego
item.description:
Maltego is known for visual link analysis. An investigator starts with an entity such as a domain name, email address, or company, then runs transforms that pull related data from sources like DNS records, social media, breach databases, and corporate registries. The results appear as a graph that shows how things connect, which makes patterns easier to see than in a list.

The tool is widely used in cybersecurity and open-source intelligence work. Threat analysts trace infrastructure behind attacks, fraud teams look for networks of related accounts, and journalists and researchers map ownership and connections. A marketplace of data integrations extends what the graph can query, and collaboration features let teams share findings.

item.title: Mangools
item.description:
Mangools packages the basic SEO jobs in friendly tools. KWFinder finds keywords and shows search volume and difficulty, SERPChecker analyzes the pages ranking for a term, SERPWatcher tracks your rankings over time, LinkMiner shows backlinks, and SiteProfiler gives an overview of a domain. Each is easy to use without deep SEO knowledge.

The strength is simplicity. Color-coded difficulty scores and clean layouts mean beginners can find a keyword worth targeting, and small agencies can report progress to clients. The tools share a login and subscription, and the company offers learning material on SEO basics.

item.title: Matillion
item.description:
Matillion is a data integration platform. Data teams use a visual designer to extract data from sources, load it into a cloud warehouse, and transform it there using the warehouse’s own compute. This ELT approach scales with the warehouse and keeps data in the company’s environment.

AI has become part of the product through Maia, a set of agents that act as virtual data engineers. A user describes what they need, and Maia can create pipelines, suggest fixes when something fails, and write documentation. Humans stay in the loop and can review the generated work. The platform also supports orchestration, scheduling, and version control with Git.

item.title: Meltano
item.description:
Meltano treats data integration like software development. A project defines extractors and loaders in a configuration file, and Meltano runs them to move data from sources into a warehouse. Because everything is code, pipelines live in Git, run in CI, and can be reviewed like other changes.

It builds on the Singer standard, which has hundreds of community connectors, and integrates with dbt for transformations and Airflow for orchestration. Teams can write custom connectors with a software development kit, which is handy for sources that commercial tools do not cover.

item.title: Mendeley
item.description:
Mendeley helps researchers organize the papers they read. Users import PDFs, and the software extracts details such as the title and authors, stores them in a library, and lets them highlight and annotate. A Word plugin inserts citations and builds a reference list in thousands of styles, which saves hours when writing papers and theses.

It has social and discovery elements, including groups for sharing libraries and a catalog of research papers. Syncing across the desktop, web, and mobile keeps a library available wherever you work. Elsevier acquired the company, which led some researchers to prefer open alternatives because of concerns about data and lock-in.

item.title: Microsoft Clarity
item.description:
Clarity shows how people really use a website. A snippet of code installed on the site captures sessions, which can be replayed like a video, along with heatmaps that show where visitors click and how far they scroll. It automatically flags signs of frustration, including rage clicks, dead clicks, excessive scrolling, and JavaScript errors, so teams can focus on pages where users struggle.

AI features add convenience. Copilot summarizes many sessions to surface common issues and gives answers to questions about user behavior, and filters let you segment by device, country, and traffic source. Clarity also offers insights on how AI chatbots and search drive traffic to a site. It integrates with Google Analytics, Microsoft Advertising, and platforms such as Shopify and WordPress.

item.title: Mighty Networks
item.description:
Mighty Networks is a platform for building a membership community. A creator sets up a space with feeds, groups, live events, and online courses, and members join by paying a subscription or one-time fee. The pitch is an experience that feels like your own app, with mobile apps that can carry your brand.

Monetization is built in. Creators can charge for memberships, courses, and events, offer tiered access, and run bundles. The AI assistant helps with tasks such as naming a community, drafting posts and course outlines, and suggesting engagement ideas. Analytics show member activity, which helps community managers improve retention.

item.title: Mixpanel
item.description:
Mixpanel helps product teams understand behavior. You send events from your product, such as sign-ups, searches, and purchases, along with properties about users, and Mixpanel turns them into reports. Funnels show where people drop off, retention charts show who comes back, flows map the paths people take, and cohorts group users by behavior. Self-serve reports let product managers and marketers answer questions without writing SQL.

The platform includes more than charts. Session replay shows what users actually did, feature flags and experiments test changes, and lexicon tools manage the data schema. AI features let people ask questions in plain language and generate reports, summarize findings, and surface anomalies. Data can be connected from warehouses, and Mixpanel integrates with tools for marketing, support, and customer data pipelines.

item.title: MX
item.description:
MX is a financial data platform. It gathers account and transaction data from thousands of institutions, enriches it by cleaning merchant names and categorizing spending, and delivers it to banks, credit unions, and fintech apps that want to offer money management features.

Its products include account aggregation, a digital banking experience that institutions can embed, insights and budgeting tools, and data for lending decisions. AI improves categorization and personalization, and connections increasingly use direct bank APIs instead of screen scraping.

item.title: NeuronWriter
item.description:
NeuronWriter is a content optimization tool. A user enters a keyword, the tool analyzes the pages that rank, and it produces a list of recommended terms, questions, and headings, along with a target length. As the writer drafts in its editor, a score shows how well the content covers the topic.

It includes an AI writing assistant for outlines and drafts, internal linking suggestions, and a way to plan content around topics. Competitor analysis shows what top pages do well. Agencies use it for client content because of its pricing.

item.title: Oracle NetSuite
item.description:
NetSuite was one of the first cloud ERP systems and is widely used by growing companies. A single system runs financials, inventory, procurement, order management, billing, and customer relationship management, so departments work from the same data instead of reconciling spreadsheets. Industry editions adapt it for areas like wholesale distribution, manufacturing, retail, and software, and it supports multiple subsidiaries, currencies, and tax rules, which suits companies expanding internationally.

AI features sit across the suite. Generative tools can summarize records, draft emails and descriptions, and answer questions about data in plain language, while machine learning supports forecasting, anomaly detection, and automation of accounting tasks like matching invoices. Reporting and analytics tools let finance teams build dashboards, and SuiteScript and workflows allow customization.

item.title: Pendo
item.description:
Pendo helps product teams understand and improve their software. After adding a snippet to an application, Pendo records usage automatically: which pages and features people use, where they drop off, and how behavior varies by customer or segment. Product managers use dashboards, funnels, and retention reports to decide what to build and what to fix.

The platform lets teams act on insights without waiting for developers. In-app guides, tooltips, announcements, and checklists guide users through features, surveys and NPS collect feedback, and a roadmap tool captures feature requests. Session replay shows what people did, and AI features summarize feedback, suggest improvements, and analyze conversations with AI features inside products, which is a growing need as software adds assistants.

item.title: Pigment
item.description:
Pigment is a modern take on planning software. Finance teams build models of their company, including headcount, revenue, and spend, in an environment that feels familiar to spreadsheet users but works with large data volumes and multiple dimensions. Plans link across departments, so a hiring plan updates the budget automatically.

It supports scenario planning, which lets teams test the impact of different assumptions side by side, and produces dashboards and reports for executives. AI agents help analyze variances, generate commentary, and build parts of models from prompts. Integrations bring in data from ERP and CRM systems and data warehouses.

item.title: Plausible
item.description:
Plausible keeps analytics simple. A tiny script collects page views, visitors, referrers, devices, and locations without using cookies or storing personal data, so most sites do not need a consent banner for it. The dashboard fits on a single page, which makes it quick to read for people who don’t want to learn a complex tool.

It supports goals and events, so site owners can track signups or purchases, and funnels for conversion steps. Features like UTM tracking and a stats API round out the basics. The code is open source, and users can self-host a free community edition or pay for the hosted service, which is run from European servers.

item.title: Qlik
item.description: Qlik is known for its associative engine, which treats all the data in an app as connected. When you click a value in a chart, everything else updates to show related data, and values that are unrelated are shown as excluded, which helps users discover connections they did not think to query. This differs from tools that require predefined queries and has been a selling point for business users exploring data.

item.title: Questel
item.description:
Questel serves people who work with patents and trademarks. Its search tools let users query large databases of patents from many countries, apply classifications, and find prior art for patentability and infringement questions. Analytics show landscapes of who is filing in a field and trends over time.

The company also offers portfolio management, with docketing, renewals, and workflow tools for tracking deadlines across jurisdictions, along with services for filing and annuity payments. AI features assist with semantic search, summarization, and drafting, helping professionals review large numbers of documents faster. Its products come from combining several IP software companies.

item.title: SAP Concur
item.description:
Concur is a staple of corporate finance. Employees book travel, capture receipts with a phone, and submit expense reports, which flow through approvals and into accounting systems. Policies are applied automatically, flagging out-of-policy spending, and credit card feeds reduce manual entry. Finance teams use it to control costs, reimburse employees, and meet audit requirements.

The platform has grown to include invoice and travel management, with integrations to airlines, hotels, and payment providers. AI supports automatic receipt reading, categorization, audit of expenses to detect errors or fraud, and assistance through SAP’s Joule for answering questions and completing tasks. Reporting provides visibility into travel and spending trends.

item.title: Scopus
item.description:
Scopus indexes scholarly journals, books, and conference papers across science, technology, medicine, social sciences, and the arts and humanities, and tracks citations among them. Researchers use it to search literature, follow citation trails, and find related work. It’s curated: content must meet quality criteria to be included, which gives the database a reputation for reliability.

Institutions rely on Scopus for research evaluation. It provides author profiles with h-index and other metrics, journal rankings such as CiteScore, and tools for analyzing the output of departments and universities. Funders and universities use these numbers in assessments, rankings, and hiring, which makes the database influential, and sometimes controversial because of the weight put on metrics.

item.title: Skool
item.description:
Skool is a simple platform for running a community. Members post in a feed, take courses in a classroom section, attend events from a shared calendar, and earn points for participating, which unlock levels on a leaderboard. The gamification is meant to keep people engaged without a lot of setup.

The pricing and design are deliberately simple. Skool charges a flat fee for community owners and offers few customization options, so creators spend time on content and members, not on configuring a site. Communities can charge a monthly or annual fee, and a built-in discovery page, plus members’ direct messages, helps people find groups.

item.title: SpyFu
item.description:
SpyFu is a competitor research tool. Enter a domain and it reveals the keywords that site ranks for in organic search, the keywords it buys on Google Ads, and how those change over time. The ad history is a distinctive feature, since you can see which ad copy a competitor has tested and kept running.

That data helps marketers decide where to compete. Keyword research shows search volume and difficulty, backlink tools find link opportunities, and rank tracking monitors progress. Agencies use the reports to pitch clients, and PPC managers use the ad history to find ideas and gaps in their own campaigns.

item.title: Streamlit
item.description: Streamlit is built for data scientists who want to share work without learning web development. You write a Python script and add calls like text input, sliders, charts, and buttons, and Streamlit produces an interactive web app that reruns the script when the user changes something. This model is simple enough that people can make an app in minutes, and it has become a standard for internal tools and demos.

item.title: SurveyMonkey
item.description:
SurveyMonkey is one of the best-known survey tools. Users create surveys with a drag-and-drop builder, choose from templates for customer satisfaction, employee engagement, market research, and events, and share them by link, email, or embedding. Question logic, branching, and randomization allow more sophisticated designs, and responses appear in real time with charts and filters.

AI features aim to make surveys better and analysis quicker. The assistant can build a survey from a description, suggest improved wording to avoid bias, and analyze open-ended responses by identifying themes and sentiment. A panel service lets researchers purchase responses from target audiences, and integrations connect results to tools like Salesforce, Slack, and Tableau.

item.title: TubeBuddy
item.description:
TubeBuddy is a browser extension and mobile app for YouTube creators. It adds tools to the YouTube interface, including a keyword explorer that estimates how competitive a search term is, tag suggestions, and a score that shows how well a video is optimized. These help creators choose topics and fill in titles and descriptions with search in mind.

Other features save time. Bulk tools update many videos at once, thumbnail A/B testing compares designs for click rates, and scheduling and reminders organize publishing. Analytics show how a channel performs and how it compares to others. AI tools suggest titles, descriptions, and ideas based on a video’s topic.

item.title: Vertex
item.description:
Vertex helps businesses get sales and use tax, VAT, and similar indirect taxes right. When a company sells a product, the right tax depends on the buyer’s location, the product type, and applicable rules, which change often. Vertex maintains a large database of rates and rules, and its engine calculates the correct tax inside systems like SAP, Oracle, and Microsoft Dynamics.

The company also covers filing and reporting. Tools prepare returns, manage exemption certificates, and support e-invoicing mandates that countries are introducing. AI features help classify products to the right tax codes and speed up compliance work. Customers are mostly large enterprises with complex tax footprints across many jurisdictions.

item.title: Vidyard
item.description:
Vidyard is a video platform for business teams. Salespeople record quick webcam or screen videos for prospects, send them by email or link, and see who watched and for how long. Marketers host videos on their websites with branded players and gated forms.

AI features speed up production. Script suggestions help with what to say, avatars let a rep send a personalized video without recording each one, and transcripts, summaries, and chapters make longer videos easier to use. Integrations with Salesforce and HubSpot put engagement data in the CRM.

item.title: Vimeo
item.description:
Vimeo started as a community for filmmakers and grew into a professional video platform. Businesses use it to host and share video without ads, embed customizable players on their websites, control who can watch, and see analytics on viewing. Features such as review tools, live streaming, and webinars support marketing, training, and internal communications.

AI features have been added to speed up work. Tools can generate scripts, create video from text or slides, produce captions and translations, and edit footage by removing filler words or creating highlights, and an AI assistant helps with chapters and summaries. Vimeo’s editing tools and recording app allow teams to produce video without separate software.

item.title: Web of Science
item.description:
Web of Science is one of the oldest and most influential indexes of scholarly literature. It covers curated sets of journals, conference proceedings, and books and records which works cite which, making it possible to follow ideas forward and backward through the literature. Researchers use it to find relevant papers, track citations, and analyze trends in a field.

Institutions also use its data for research evaluation. Clarivate publishes the Journal Citation Reports, which includes the impact factor, one of the most discussed metrics in academia, and Web of Science supports measures of authors, journals, and institutions. A Research Assistant adds AI-driven features such as natural language search and summaries of results. The selectivity of coverage is a selling point and also a criticism, as it favors certain journals and languages.

item.title: Wrike
item.description:
Wrike is used by teams that coordinate lots of work. Projects can be viewed as lists, boards, Gantt charts, or calendars, and tasks carry dependencies, owners, due dates, and custom fields. Request forms and approvals let outside teams submit work in a structured way, which helps marketing, creative, and operations groups manage intake.

AI features reduce routine effort. Wrike’s tools can summarize long comment threads, create tasks from text, draft project descriptions, and predict which projects are at risk of missing deadlines. Dashboards show workloads and progress across portfolios, and integrations connect to Slack, Salesforce, Microsoft 365, and Adobe tools. Proofing helps creative teams review assets.

item.title: Xero
item.description:
Xero is an online accounting platform used widely in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, and increasingly elsewhere. Business owners and bookkeepers connect their bank accounts so transactions flow in automatically, then match them to invoices and bills in a reconciliation process that Xero makes quick with suggested matches. It generates invoices, tracks expenses and cash flow, and produces reports such as profit and loss and balance sheets.

An accountant-friendly design is part of its appeal. Unlimited users on most plans let owners, bookkeepers, and accountants work in the same file, and a large marketplace of integrations connects Xero to payment providers, payroll, inventory, and point-of-sale systems. AI features include suggested coding of transactions, predictive cash flow tools, and an assistant for asking questions about the business and automating tasks like drafting invoice reminders.

item.title: YNAB
item.description:
YNAB is as much a method as an app. Users assign each dollar of income to a category, such as rent, groceries, or savings, and update the plan as real spending happens. When money moves between categories, the app shows the tradeoff. The idea is to work from money you already have, not money you expect, which many people find reduces financial stress.

Features support that approach. Bank syncing imports transactions, goals track bills and savings targets, reports show spending trends, and shared budgets let partners manage money together. The company offers workshops and guides that teach the approach, which is a big part of why users stick with it. There is a mobile app and a web version.

item.title: Ancestry
item.description:
Ancestry is a genealogy service. Users build a family tree and the site suggests matching records, such as birth certificates, census pages, immigration lists, and military files, from its collection. Hints appear as you add relatives, which helps trace lines back through generations.

Technology helps both records and relatives. Handwriting recognition and machine learning transcribe old documents so they become searchable, and the DNA test connects users with genetic relatives and estimates ethnic origins. Members can share trees and message distant cousins, which often breaks through research dead ends.

item.title: Blend
item.description:
Blend builds software for lenders. Instead of paper forms and email, borrowers apply on a digital platform that collects information, connects to bank accounts and payroll sources to verify income and assets, and tracks the status of the application. Loan officers and processors see the file in a shared workflow.

Automation cuts the manual work in underwriting preparation. The platform pulls data from verified sources, checks documents, and flags missing or inconsistent items so staff can fix problems early. It covers mortgages, home equity, and consumer lending products, and integrates with loan origination systems and credit providers.

item.title: Circle
item.description:
Circle gives communities a home of their own. A creator sets up spaces for topics, posts content, hosts live events, runs courses, and lets members message each other, all under a custom domain and brand. It aims to feel more focused than a social network and less cluttered than a forum.

Monetization is built in. Communities can charge for memberships, offer paid tiers, and sell courses and events, with workflows to onboard new members. AI features draft welcome messages, summarize conversations, and help members find information, while analytics show engagement and which members are most active. Mobile apps and integrations with tools like Zapier extend reach.

item.title: Daloopa
item.description:
Daloopa serves the finance professionals who build models from public company reports. Instead of typing numbers from filings into Excel, an analyst gets a database of financial line items pulled from documents like quarterly reports and presentations, with each number linked back to its source in the original file.

Updates arrive soon after companies report, so models stay current. An Excel add-in lets analysts pull data into their own templates, and an API and integrations with AI assistants allow data to flow into other workflows. The company has focused on accuracy and traceability, since errors in financial data are costly.

item.title: Floify
item.description:
Floify handles the document stage of mortgage lending. Loan officers invite borrowers to a secure portal where they upload pay stubs, bank statements, and other items, sign disclosures electronically, and watch the status of their loan. The portal carries the lender’s branding.

Automation reduces manual follow-up. The system sends reminders for missing documents, sorts and labels uploads, and updates borrowers and real estate agents as milestones are reached. It connects to loan origination systems so data moves between them. Analytics show where loans get stuck.

item.title: Hunchly
item.description:
Hunchly is a browser extension for investigations. As a researcher browses, it saves each page as it appeared, with screenshots, timestamps, and hash values that help show the content has not been altered. Pages are organized into cases, so evidence from a long investigation stays together.

The tool adds notes, tags, and a way to search across captured content. Reports can be generated for sharing or for legal use. It is popular with open-source intelligence investigators, journalists, and fraud and law enforcement analysts who need to preserve content that may disappear.

item.title: Kentik
item.description:
Kentik gives network teams insight into how traffic moves. It collects flow records, routing information, and metrics from routers, switches, and cloud networks, stores them at large scale, and lets engineers query who is talking to whom and how much. That helps with capacity planning, troubleshooting, and cost control.

Security and reliability uses include detecting DDoS attacks and unusual traffic patterns, analyzing BGP routing changes, and finding the reason for a slowdown across multiple networks. An AI assistant lets users ask questions in plain language and speeds up root cause analysis. Cloud and data center networks are covered.

item.title: LeanTaaS
item.description:
LeanTaaS builds software for healthcare capacity. Hospitals struggle with uneven demand: operating rooms sit idle while patients wait, infusion chairs are overbooked on some days, and beds are not available when needed. LeanTaaS forecasts demand and recommends schedules that balance resources and reduce wait times.

Its iQueue products cover operating rooms, infusion centers, and inpatient beds. Algorithms assess historical patterns and help staff adjust block time, appointment slots, and staffing. Improvements can increase the number of patients served without adding space.

item.title: Muck Rack
item.description:
Muck Rack is a public relations platform. PR professionals search its database to find journalists who cover a topic, see what they have written recently, and build media lists. They send pitches and track responses, and the platform monitors news to show where their company or clients are mentioned.

Reporting tools measure coverage by reach and sentiment, and dashboards show how campaigns perform. AI features summarize articles, suggest journalists, and help draft pitches, saving time on research and writing. The company also publishes research about the relationship between journalists and PR.

item.title: MyHeritage
item.description:
MyHeritage is a genealogy service. Users create a tree, and the site suggests matches in historical records and in other members’ trees, helping them find ancestors and living relatives. A DNA test adds ethnicity estimates and connects users with genetic relatives.

The company is known for photo tools. It can colorize black-and-white pictures, enhance old photos, and animate faces in family photographs, which went viral and made genealogy more emotional for many users. Other AI features transcribe and search documents.

item.title: nCino
item.description:
nCino is cloud banking software. A bank uses it to manage the full lending process, from application to documents, analysis, approval, and closing, replacing paper and email chains. It covers commercial, consumer, and mortgage lending and account opening.

AI and automation reduce manual work. Models extract financial data from documents, assess credit risk, and flag items for review, and agents help with tasks like drafting credit memos. Dashboards give management visibility across the portfolio.

item.title: Propeller Aero
item.description:
Propeller serves construction, mining, and quarry sites. A drone flies a site, often with ground control targets, and the images are processed into accurate maps and 3D models. Users measure stockpiles, cut and fill volumes, and compare the site with design plans.

Dashboards share progress with project teams, and tools track haul roads, compare surveys over time, and generate reports for clients. Its PPK-enabled hardware and workflow aim to improve accuracy and reduce the need for ground control points.

item.title: Rayyan
item.description:
Rayyan streamlines a laborious step in evidence synthesis. Researchers import search results from databases, and multiple reviewers screen titles and abstracts, marking papers as included or excluded, often blind to each other’s decisions. The tool tracks conflicts and helps resolve them.

Machine learning ranks the unscreened papers by likelihood of relevance, so the likely includes surface earlier and screening can end sooner. Highlighting of keywords and filtering by terms speeds reading. Newer features use AI to assist with extraction and summaries.

item.title: Reaxys
item.description:
Reaxys is a chemistry research database from Elsevier. A chemist can search by structure, reaction, or property and find experimental data on compounds, along with the reactions used to make them and the sources. This helps plan syntheses and avoid repeating known work.

Predictive synthesis tools propose routes to a target molecule by combining literature data with machine learning, ranking options by feasibility. It also covers properties, bioactivity, and patent chemistry, serving drug discovery and materials work.

item.title: Rogo
item.description:
Rogo focuses on the work of junior bankers and analysts, who spend hours digging through filings, transcripts, and data. A user asks a question in plain language, such as how a company’s margins compare with peers, and Rogo retrieves and analyzes the sources, citing where numbers came from.

It connects to financial data providers and a firm’s internal documents, produces outputs like comps and summaries, and fits into the workflow with tools such as Excel and PowerPoint. Security and compliance features suit regulated firms.

item.title: Sales Boomerang
item.description:
Sales Boomerang helps brokers stay in touch at the right time. It connects to a broker’s client list, watches for signals such as changes in credit, equity, or market rates, and alerts the broker when a former client might benefit from refinancing or a new purchase.

That turns a dormant database into leads. Automated outreach can follow, with messages personalized to the situation. Brokers use it to generate repeat and referral business without constant manual review.

item.title: Vagaro
item.description:
Vagaro runs the front desk for beauty and wellness businesses. Clients book online or through a marketplace app, staff manage calendars, take payments, and track inventory. Reminders and no-show protection reduce lost appointments.

Marketing tools include email and text campaigns, loyalty programs, and a presence on the Vagaro marketplace. AI answers calls and messages, helps book appointments, and suggests promotions.

Vagaro charges a monthly fee per business, with add-ons and payment processing fees. Alternatives include Fresha, Booksy, StyleSeat, Square Appointments, and Mindbody. Vagaro suits salons, spas, and studios.

item.title: VidIQ
item.description:
vidIQ helps YouTubers grow. A browser extension adds data to YouTube pages and Studio, showing keyword scores, competitor stats, and tags used by successful videos. Research tools find topics with demand and low competition.

AI features suggest video ideas, titles, and thumbnails, write descriptions, and give feedback on videos. Analytics track subscriber growth and performance, and a coach feature gives guidance.

vidIQ has a free plan and paid tiers. Optimization scores are guides, and content quality drives results. Alternatives include TubeBuddy, Morningfame, Social Blade, and YouTube’s own research tools. vidIQ suits creators optimizing a channel.

item.title: Visier
item.description:
Visier gathers data from HR systems into a model built for workforce questions. HR teams and managers explore metrics such as turnover, hiring speed, diversity, and compensation, and see how they vary by team and over time. Prebuilt analyses save the effort of building reports from scratch.

AI predicts who may leave, models the effect of decisions, and answers questions in plain language through a virtual assistant. Planning tools support headcount and cost scenarios, and integrations pull data from systems such as Workday and SAP.

item.title: QueryStory
item.description:
QueryStory approaches analytics with agents. A team connects its data sources and describes the business, such as its metrics and definitions, and then asks questions in natural language. The agents write queries, analyze results, and respond with explanations and visuals.

The point is to go beyond a static chart. When a number moves, a user can ask why, and the agent investigates by looking at breakdowns and related data. Business context helps the agent interpret questions the way an analyst on the team would.

item.title: Viktor
item.description:
Viktor lives where teams already talk. Instead of a separate app, a colleague mentions Viktor in a channel and asks for something, such as pulling numbers from a dashboard, building a report, or writing a script, and it replies in the thread. It watches how the team works and picks up context over time.

It connects to a very large number of business tools, so it can read from and act in systems like CRMs, analytics, and ad platforms, and it can produce artifacts such as documents and simple web apps. Skills can be added for specialized work.

item.title: BrowserStack Test Companion
item.description:
Test Companion is an AI agent for quality assurance. Instead of a separate dashboard, it works in the developer’s editor, where it can generate test scripts from a description or from the code, run them on BrowserStack’s device and browser cloud, and investigate failures.

Maintenance is a major use. Tests break when interfaces change, and fixing them takes time. The agent can update selectors, adjust steps, and rerun, which reduces the upkeep that makes automated testing costly. It works with common frameworks and connects to BrowserStack’s testing infrastructure.

item.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway
item.description:
AI Gateway is a proxy for calls to language models. A developer points their app’s requests at a Cloudflare URL instead of the provider’s, and the gateway forwards them while recording what happens. This gives a dashboard of requests, tokens, costs, and errors across providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

It adds control features. Caching returns stored answers for repeated requests to save money and time, rate limits protect budgets, and retries and fallbacks switch to another model when one fails. Logging helps debug prompts, and guardrails and key management features support security.

item.title: Cohere North
item.description:
North is Cohere’s platform for putting agents to work inside companies. Employees use a chat interface and can build agents without code for tasks in HR, finance, IT, and other areas, connecting them to the apps and documents they already use. Search across company data is powered by Cohere’s own retrieval technology.

Security and control are the main pitch. Organizations can deploy North in a private cloud, on premises, or in air-gapped settings, which appeals to banks, governments, and defense contractors with strict data rules. Cohere designs the models for enterprise use and works with customers on custom solutions.

item.title: Dataiku
item.description:
Dataiku aims to let analysts, data scientists, and engineers work in the same environment. Teams connect to data sources, clean and prepare data with visual recipes or code, build models, and deploy them as applications or services. The visual interface lowers the barrier for business users, while coders can use notebooks and libraries.

The platform has added tools for generative AI, including connecting to language models, building retrieval applications, and creating agents. Governance features track models and projects, assess risk, and document decisions, which large organizations need to meet internal and regulatory requirements.

item.title: SwiftAlerts
item.description:
SwiftAlerts gathers market data into a structure that agents can query. Instead of hunting through separate sources, an agent can ask about relationships between trades, holdings, filings, and sentiment, and get connected answers.

The idea fits the rise of AI agents that research and monitor markets. Reliable data is essential, since trading decisions on wrong information lose money, and nothing from such a tool is financial advice.

Independent information is limited, so check data sources, update speed, and terms. SwiftAlerts is free to start. Alternatives include Unusual Whales, Quiver Quantitative, Benzinga, Polygon.io, and Financial Datasets. SwiftAlerts suits developers building market agents, with caution.

item.title: Anomaly AI
item.description:
Anomaly AI is for people who work with data that is too big or messy for a normal spreadsheet. A user uploads Excel or CSV files or connects sources such as databases, warehouses, and Google Sheets, then asks questions in natural language. The tool answers with tables, charts, and written explanations.

The vendor emphasizes traceable answers, meaning the analysis is run as code against the data so results can be inspected and not just generated by a language model. It can merge files with database data in one analysis, find trends, and flag unusual values. A connector allows assistants like Claude to hand questions about your data to the service.

item.title: Alli AI
item.description:
Alli AI addresses a common obstacle in SEO: implementing recommended changes often requires developer time. Alli installs a snippet on a website, and then SEO teams can edit and push on-page elements, such as titles, meta descriptions, headings, schema markup, and internal links, directly from its dashboard to many pages at once. Changes can be tested and rolled back, and the platform tracks results.

AI features suggest optimizations. The tool analyzes pages and recommends improvements, can generate titles and descriptions in bulk, and automates tasks such as adding structured data. Agencies value it for managing many client sites through one interface, and enterprises use it to speed up large-scale optimization where release cycles are slow.

item.title: Databricks
item.description:
Databricks started with Apache Spark and grew into a unified platform for data work. Companies store data in open formats in their cloud, then use Databricks for pipelines, SQL analytics, notebooks, and machine learning, with a governance layer called Unity Catalog that controls access and tracks lineage across it all.

AI has become central to the pitch. The platform supports training and fine-tuning models, serving them through endpoints, vector search for retrieval, and a framework for building agents grounded in enterprise data. The company acquired MosaicML to strengthen model training, and offers tools to monitor and evaluate AI systems. An assistant helps write code and queries.

item.title: Glassbox
item.description:
Glassbox captures user sessions on digital properties. Teams can replay a visit to see what a customer clicked, where they hesitated, and what errors they hit. Heatmaps summarize click and scroll behavior across many sessions, pointing to confusing pages or broken flows.

The platform adds analytics and detection. Journey analysis shows where users leave a funnel, and automatic detection flags frustration signals such as repeated clicks. It has features for regulated industries like banking, including data masking so that sensitive information is not stored. The company has expanded through acquisitions into areas like anomaly detection.

item.title: Hex
item.description:
Hex combines notebooks with business intelligence. Teams connect their data warehouse, write SQL and Python in a notebook, and turn the results into interactive apps that non-technical colleagues can use without code. Everything lives in one place with version history and comments.

AI is built into the workflow. Magic helps write and fix queries and code, and agents let business users ask questions of governed data in plain language. A semantic layer keeps definitions of metrics consistent, so answers match across reports. Scheduled runs keep outputs fresh.

item.title: Highspot
item.description:
Highspot helps sales organizations make sure reps find and use the right material. Marketing publishes decks, case studies, and playbooks in one library, reps search or get recommendations based on the deal stage and customer, and managers see which assets are used and which correlate with wins.

Training and coaching tools are part of the platform, including practice exercises, call reviews, and guided selling plays. AI features recommend content, summarize accounts, and generate tailored messages and presentations. Integrations with CRMs and communication tools bring this into reps’ daily workflow.

item.title: Instapage
item.description:
Instapage focuses on the page that visitors reach after clicking an ad. Marketers build pages in a drag-and-drop editor with templates, connect them to ad campaigns, and track conversion rates. Collaboration features let teams and clients comment directly on designs.

Optimization tools set it apart. A/B testing compares versions, heatmaps show where visitors engage, and personalization changes page content depending on the ad or audience that sent the visitor. AI helps write copy and suggests improvements.

item.title: Keyword Insights
item.description:
Keyword Insights helps turn a long keyword list into a content plan. A user uploads thousands of keywords or discovers them in the tool, and the platform clusters them based on how search results overlap, which indicates whether a group of terms should be targeted by one page or several.

It also determines search intent for each cluster, suggests content types, and produces briefs that outline what a page should cover based on top results. Rank tracking and content tools support the workflow after publishing, and AI assists with drafting.

item.title: Laxis
item.description:
Laxis joins online meetings, records and transcribes them, and produces summaries with action items and key points. Sales teams use it to log call notes in the CRM automatically, and researchers and recruiters use it for interviews. Search across past meetings helps find specific topics.

Extra features include templates for different meeting types, follow-up email drafts, and analytics on conversations. Integrations connect with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and CRMs such as Salesforce and HubSpot.

item.title: MotherDuck
item.description:
MotherDuck takes the DuckDB analytical database, which runs on a laptop, and adds a cloud service. A user connects from their local DuckDB, queries data in the cloud, and combines it with local files, in what the company calls hybrid execution, using each machine for what it does best.

It targets teams that do not need a large data warehouse. Features include shared databases, collaboration, integrations with common data tools, and an AI assistant that helps write SQL. The pitch is simple, fast analytics at lower cost for data in the gigabytes to terabytes range.

item.title: Planable
item.description:
Planable is built around approval workflows. Marketers create posts in a view that looks like the final social post, share it with teammates or clients, collect comments and approvals, and schedule it once signed off. This replaces long email chains and screenshots.

Features include a content calendar, multiple approval stages, and support for many networks. AI tools help draft captions and ideas. Agencies find it useful for client work where sign-off is required.

item.title: Seismic
item.description:
Seismic organizes marketing and sales content so reps can find and use it. Instead of searching shared drives, a seller gets recommended decks, case studies, and playbooks based on the deal stage and customer, and can assemble personalized presentations quickly.

Analytics show which content gets used and which correlates with wins, and engagement data tells sellers how buyers interact with shared materials. Coaching and training modules, and AI that writes tailored messages and summaries, add to the suite.

item.title: Snowflake
item.description:
Snowflake pioneered the cloud data warehouse built on this separation. Companies load data, run SQL queries with elastic compute, and share datasets securely with partners. It runs on the major clouds, and teams of analysts and engineers use it as a central data foundation.

The platform has grown into an AI data cloud. Cortex provides language model functions, search over documents, and agents that run inside the platform, close to the data, with governance. It also supports machine learning, Python workloads, and apps built on Snowflake data.

item.title: Sprinklr
item.description:
Sprinklr serves very large organizations. It manages publishing across social channels, listens for brand mentions, handles customer care across messaging and voice, and analyzes market trends, using a shared data layer so teams see the whole customer picture.

AI runs through the platform: models classify conversations, detect sentiment, route cases, suggest replies, and generate content, and agents handle some customer interactions. Governance tools suit regulated industries and large teams.

Sprinklr is sold on enterprise subscriptions, with high cost and complexity. Alternatives include Hootsuite, Sprout Social, Khoros, Emplifi, and Salesforce. Sprinklr suits large brands managing many channels.

item.title: Talkwalker
item.description:
Talkwalker monitors the public conversation about brands and topics. Users set up searches, and the platform collects posts, articles, forums, and broadcast mentions from around the world, then analyzes volume, sentiment, and who is talking. Alerts flag spikes that may signal a crisis or opportunity.

Image and video recognition detect logos in pictures even when the brand name is not written, and AI summarizes themes and trends. Marketing and communications teams use the findings to measure campaigns, track competitors, and shape messaging, and a generative assistant helps analysts query the data.

item.title: Transistor
item.description:
Transistor is designed for people who run more than one podcast. A single account can host unlimited shows, which suits agencies, companies, and networks, and plans are based on downloads and team size instead of per-show fees. Episodes distribute to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other apps through an RSS feed Transistor manages.

Other features address professional needs. Private podcasts let companies share internal or members-only audio, embeddable players and a branded website help promote shows, and detailed analytics show downloads and audience. Collaboration features give team members access to specific shows, and integrations connect with Zapier and other tools. AI tools support transcripts and episode copy.

item.title: Looker
item.description:
Looker takes a modeling-first approach. Data teams define dimensions and measures in LookML, a code-based language, and users explore data and build dashboards on top of those shared definitions. This keeps numbers consistent and cuts arguments over whose revenue figure is right.

The platform queries data warehouses directly, so it works with the company’s data without extracting it. It supports embedded analytics, letting companies put dashboards in their own products. Gemini in Looker adds conversational analytics and help writing LookML and building reports.

item.title: Meltwater
item.description:
Meltwater is a media monitoring and social listening platform. Users set up searches for brand names, competitors, and topics, and the system collects mentions from news sites, blogs, social networks, forums, and broadcast sources, with alerts and dashboards.

Analytics show volume, sentiment, and reach, and AI highlights trends and unusual spikes, such as the start of a negative story. Tools for PR teams include media databases for finding journalists, and distribution of press releases. Reports demonstrate the impact of campaigns.

item.title: Qualtrics
item.description:
Qualtrics is an experience management platform. Organizations use it to run customer satisfaction surveys, product research, brand studies, and employee engagement programs. A powerful survey builder handles complex logic, and results flow into dashboards segmented by customer, team, or time.

AI features turn feedback into action. They analyze comments for sentiment and themes, spot issues as they emerge, predict which customers may leave, and suggest next steps. The platform also pulls in data from support calls, reviews, and social media.

item.title: EnergyCAP
item.description:
EnergyCAP collects utility bills and meter data and puts them into one system. Facility managers, energy consultants, and sustainability teams use it to track electricity, gas, water, and other utilities across a portfolio, pay bills, and report on costs and emissions.

Analytics find savings. The software flags bills with errors, such as duplicate charges or wrong rates, and highlights usage that departs from normal patterns, which may point to equipment problems. Benchmarking compares buildings, and reports support sustainability disclosures and incentive programs.

item.title: ESO
item.description:
ESO makes software for emergency medical services and fire departments. Paramedics record patient information, vitals, treatments, and outcomes on a tablet or laptop, producing the patient care report that is shared with hospitals and used for billing and quality review.

AI helps reduce documentation time. The software can draft narrative sections from the structured data a medic entered, and flag missing or inconsistent items so reports are complete. The company also sells products for hospitals, health data analytics, and fire records management.

item.title: ArcGIS
item.description: ArcGIS is the leading commercial GIS platform. Governments, utilities, environmental agencies, city planners, and businesses use it to collect location data, display it on maps, and analyze spatial relationships, such as which neighborhoods lie within a flood zone or where to place a new store. The product family includes ArcGIS Pro for desktop analysis, ArcGIS Online as a cloud service for building and sharing maps, and ArcGIS Enterprise for organizations that run their own servers.

item.title: Azure IoT Hub
item.description: Azure IoT Hub is the messaging backbone for connected devices on Azure. Devices send telemetry such as sensor readings to the cloud, and the cloud can send commands and configuration back. Each device has its own identity and credentials, so the platform can authenticate it, and connections use standard protocols like MQTT and AMQP. The hub scales to large fleets and can route messages to storage, stream processing, and analytics services.

item.title: Benchling
item.description: Benchling brings the scattered tasks of a research lab into one cloud system. Scientists use the notebook to record experiments, design DNA and protein sequences with molecular biology tools, and register the samples and materials they create, so everything is traceable. Teams track workflows, share results, and connect lab instruments, which replaces a mix of spreadsheets, paper notebooks, and separate databases. It is common at startups and large biopharma companies.

item.title: Bizzabo
item.description: Bizzabo is a software platform for corporate and large-scale event teams. Planners build event websites, sell tickets and handle registration, manage speakers and agendas, and track who attends. On site, it supports badge printing and check-in, and a mobile app lets attendees see the schedule, message each other, and use polls or Q&A during sessions. For virtual and hybrid events, it can stream sessions and bring remote attendees into the same experience.

item.title: Bloomerang
item.description: Bloomerang is built around donor retention, which is one of the hardest problems in fundraising: many donors give once and never again. The CRM stores each supporter’s contact details, gifts, communications, and notes, and it shows a timeline of every interaction. A generosity score and engagement level help staff see who is likely to give again and who may be slipping away, so they can focus outreach where it counts.

item.title: Datadog
item.description: Datadog is software-as-a-service for watching what your systems are doing. You install an agent on servers, containers, or cloud accounts, or connect it through one of hundreds of integrations, and it begins collecting metrics, logs, and traces. Dashboards and alerts then show how hosts, databases, queues, and services are behaving. The value for most teams is having infrastructure monitoring, application performance monitoring, log management, and real user monitoring in one place instead of stitching together separate tools.

item.title: Dune Analytics
item.description:
Dune made blockchain data accessible. Raw on-chain information is hard to work with, so Dune indexes data from many blockchains into databases that anyone can query with SQL. Users write queries to answer questions such as how many people used a decentralized exchange last week or how much value is locked in a protocol, and publish results as charts on dashboards that others can fork and extend.

The community aspect is a key feature. Analysts share dashboards openly, so you can find ready-made views of NFT markets, stablecoin flows, protocol metrics, and more, and learn from other people’s queries. Dune AI features help generate and explain SQL from natural language, and APIs allow developers to use query results in applications. Data teams use it for research and reporting.

item.title: Fleetio
item.description:
Fleetio helps organizations that rely on vehicles keep them running. It maintains a record for every vehicle, truck, or piece of equipment, including service history, documents, and costs. Preventive maintenance schedules trigger reminders by mileage, hours, or time, which reduces breakdowns and extends vehicle life. Drivers can complete inspections on a phone app, report issues, and log fuel, and shops can manage work orders and parts.

Data from telematics devices flows into the system, so mileage, location, and diagnostic trouble codes update automatically and can trigger work orders. Reports show total cost of ownership, fuel use, downtime, and compliance items, and integrations connect with accounting, fuel card, and telematics providers. AI features help summarize issues, surface patterns, and suggest actions to reduce cost.

item.title: Flexport
item.description:
Flexport is a freight forwarder with a software platform. Companies that import and export goods book shipments, track containers, manage documents, and handle customs through a single interface, instead of coordinating by email with many parties. It also offers financing, warehousing, and trade services.

Technology handles repetitive work. AI reads shipping documents, checks customs data for errors, and predicts delays based on port, carrier, and weather information. An assistant answers questions about shipment status and helps with classification of goods. Data from many shipments feeds analytics on cost and performance.

item.title: Geotab
item.description:
Geotab makes the small devices that plug into vehicles and report what they do. A device in the diagnostic port records location, speed, harsh braking, idling, engine fault codes, and more, and sends the data to the cloud, where fleet managers view it on maps and dashboards. Companies with delivery vans, service trucks, buses, and long-haul trucks use it to track vehicles, optimize routes, and reduce costs.

Analytics turn the data into insights. Driver scoring identifies risky behavior and supports coaching, maintenance alerts flag vehicles that need service based on engine data, and fuel and emissions reports support efficiency and electric vehicle planning. AI features include an assistant that answers questions about fleet data in natural language, and models that predict problems and rank safety risks. A marketplace of third-party apps extends the platform, and compliance tools support electronic logging rules.

item.title: Honeycomb
item.description:
Honeycomb works from the premise that modern systems fail in unpredictable ways. Engineers send rich events and traces with many attributes, and can slice and filter by any of them to find what is different about slow or failing requests. High-cardinality fields such as user IDs are supported, which many tools handle poorly.

Visual tools highlight outliers, compare groups, and follow a request across services, and service level objectives alert teams when users are affected. The platform embraces OpenTelemetry for data collection, so teams can instrument once. AI features let users ask questions in natural language and help interpret data.

item.title: Hopin
item.description:
Hopin offered an all-in-one environment for online events. Organizers sold tickets, ran live sessions on a main stage, hosted breakout rooms and video networking, and set up virtual expo booths, and attendees moved between these areas as if walking around a venue. It grew explosively as conferences moved online, with large funding rounds and acquisitions of other event and streaming companies.

As in-person events returned, demand for virtual events dropped sharply, and Hopin shrank and restructured. It sold its events platform to RingCentral, which continues to operate it as part of its own offering, and the company’s other products, such as streaming and community tools, were separated or spun out. The brand is no longer the same independent business.

item.title: Hudl
item.description:
Hudl made video review standard for coaching. Teams upload game and practice footage, coaches tag plays, and players watch clips on their phones, which replaces the old routine of sitting in a film room with a stack of tapes. The platform supports many sports, including football, basketball, volleyball, and soccer, and it lets coaches create playlists, draw on video, and share feedback with individuals or groups.

The product now includes hardware and AI. Hudl’s Focus cameras automatically follow the action and record games without a camera operator, which makes video affordable for schools and clubs. AI features tag events, cut highlights, and generate statistics, and a recruiting side of Hudl helps athletes share highlights with college coaches. Separate products serve professional teams with advanced analytics and scouting data, such as through its Wyscout and Sportscode lines.

item.title: IPlytics
item.description:
IPlytics focuses on the overlap between patents and technical standards. Many technologies, from 5G to Wi-Fi to video codecs, depend on standards, and companies hold patents they declare essential to implementing them. IPlytics links patent databases with standards documents, declarations, and standardization meeting contributions, helping users understand who owns what and how influential each player is.

Typical users are IP and licensing professionals, R&D strategists, and legal teams. They use it to search for standard-essential patents, benchmark portfolios against competitors, find licensing opportunities, and see which companies are shaping emerging standards. The platform includes analytics, dashboards, and data feeds, and AI features help classify patents and find relevant documents.

item.title: Lexalytics
item.description: Lexalytics builds natural language processing for businesses that need to make sense of large amounts of text. Its Salience engine reads reviews, survey comments, support tickets, social posts, and call transcripts and returns structured information: whether the sentiment is positive or negative, which products or people are mentioned, what themes recur, and what the author intends. Analysts can then count, trend, and compare these signals instead of reading comments one by one.

item.title: Mapbox
item.description:
Mapbox is the mapping toolkit behind many apps. Developers use its SDKs to embed interactive maps in websites and in iOS and Android apps, with control over styles, layers, and data. Mapbox Studio lets designers customize map appearance, while vector tiles keep maps fast and sharp. Companies in logistics, travel, real estate, and mobility use it to show routes, locations, and live data.

The platform goes beyond display. APIs handle geocoding and search, turn-by-turn navigation, route optimization, isochrones that show how far you can get in a given time, and traffic-aware directions. A navigation SDK supports in-app guidance, and tools for working with large geospatial datasets allow analysis and visualization. Machine learning is used for features such as map matching and road data updates, and recent products add AI assistants for developers.

item.title: Mobalytics
item.description:
Mobalytics is a gaming analytics and coaching site. Players link their accounts, and the tool analyzes their games, scoring performance across areas like farming, vision, and teamfights. A profile shows trends over time and compares the player with others at their rank.

Coaching features set it apart. The platform highlights patterns in mistakes and suggests focus areas, offers guides for champions and builds, and provides an overlay with in-game tips. Premium plans add deeper analysis and AI-generated feedback.

item.title: MonkeyLearn
item.description:
MonkeyLearn let people analyze text without machine learning expertise. Teams could connect support tickets, survey responses, reviews, and social posts, pick a ready-made model for sentiment or topics, or train a custom classifier by tagging examples. Results appeared in dashboards and could be sent to spreadsheets, helpdesks, and BI tools, which made it popular with customer experience, product, and marketing teams.

Its approach was to make natural language processing approachable. A visual interface handled model creation and testing, and the API let developers add analysis to their own apps. Typical uses included tagging support requests by issue, tracking sentiment in reviews, and pulling themes from open-ended survey answers.

item.title: Nearmap
item.description:
Nearmap captures aerial photos from aircraft, covering large areas in populated regions, and refreshes them regularly. Users view and measure current imagery on a map, compare dates to see change over time, and download data for analysis.

AI turns pictures into data. Models detect features such as roof condition, solar panels, pools, vegetation, and building footprints, giving insurers, councils, and contractors information without visiting sites. The data is available through a web app, APIs, and integrations with GIS and other tools.

item.title: PatSnap
item.description:
PatSnap serves teams that need to understand the patent landscape. Its search covers a very large collection of patents and scientific literature worldwide, and semantic search finds relevant documents from a description of an invention instead of exact keywords. Users can analyze who is filing in a technology area, map clusters of related patents, track competitors, and check whether an idea has been patented before.

Several products fit different jobs. Tools help with prior art searches before filing, freedom-to-operate checks before launching a product, and landscape analysis to guide R&D strategy. AI assistants summarize patents, extract key claims, and answer questions about a technology, and workflows let teams share results and collaborate. The platform also covers non-patent literature and market information for innovation scouting.

item.title: PlanetScale
item.description:
PlanetScale brought a workflow familiar from Git to relational databases. Developers create a branch of their database schema, make changes, and merge them through a deploy request, with checks that avoid downtime. Behind that is Vitess, the sharding system created at YouTube, which lets MySQL scale horizontally across many servers. This allows growth beyond the limits of a single database machine.

Features focus on safe changes and performance. Online schema changes let teams alter large tables without locking, insights show slow queries and suggest improvements, and connection handling supports large numbers of clients. Recent products emphasize high-performance storage and have extended the platform to Postgres. AI-assisted insights help identify problematic queries, and the service integrates with popular frameworks and hosting platforms.

item.title: Procore
item.description:
Procore is one of the most widely used software platforms in construction. It gives everyone on a building project a shared place to manage drawings and documents, RFIs and submittals, daily logs, schedules, budgets, change orders, and inspections. Instead of email chains and spreadsheets, project information lives in one system with a record of who did what, which reduces disputes and rework.

The platform spans the project lifecycle, from preconstruction bidding and estimating through construction and closeout.
