Financial tools handle cost tracking, invoicing, and payments, while quality and safety modules support checklists, observations, and incident reports. A marketplace of integrations connects accounting, scheduling, and design tools. AI features help search across documents, summarize information, and automate routine tasks, and agents are being added to take on project management work.

item.title: Sight Machine
item.description:
Sight Machine tackles the data mess inside factories. Machines, sensors, and systems produce data in many formats, and plants often cannot easily combine it. Sight Machine’s platform pulls in data from equipment, quality systems, and enterprise software, standardizes it into a common model of the production process, and creates a digital twin that shows how products move through the plant.

With that foundation, teams can analyze performance. Dashboards track throughput, yield, scrap, and downtime across lines and sites, machine learning finds the factors that drive defects or slowdowns, and alerts flag issues in near real time. An AI assistant lets operators and engineers ask questions about production data in plain language, and the platform supports sustainability tracking such as energy use.

item.title: Spire Global
item.description:
Spire builds and operates a large fleet of small satellites known as nanosatellites. Instead of taking photographs, they listen: they pick up radio signals from ships, aircraft, and GPS signals bouncing off the Earth, and measure atmospheric conditions. The resulting data feeds products that track vessels around the world, monitor air traffic, and improve weather forecasts.

The business sells data and analytics as a service. Maritime customers use it to follow ships, estimate arrival times, and detect suspicious behavior, aviation customers use it for flight tracking, and meteorological agencies use radio occultation data to enhance forecasts. Spire also provides space services, building and operating satellites for customers. Machine learning supports forecasting and anomaly detection in the data, and APIs deliver it to customers’ systems.

item.title: Stats Perform
item.description:
Stats Perform collects detailed data about professional sports. Trained collectors and tracking technology record events in matches, such as passes, shots, and player positions, and the company supplies that information to broadcasters, media companies, sportsbooks, leagues, and clubs. Its Opta brand is widely seen in football statistics on television and websites. The data feeds power live scores, fantasy games, and graphics.

AI is used both to create data and to analyze it. Computer vision extracts player and ball tracking from video, which reduces the manual work of collecting information, and models predict outcomes, evaluate player performance, and estimate the value of actions on the field. Coaches and analysts use the tools for scouting and tactical analysis, while media and betting clients use predictions and content such as automated match summaries.

item.title: StoryChief
item.description:
StoryChief helps marketing teams run a content workflow in one place. Teams plan content on a calendar, write articles in a shared editor, route them through review and approval, and then publish to multiple channels with a click, including their website, social networks, newsletters, and platforms like Medium. It reduces the work of copying content between tools and keeps assets organized.

SEO and analytics features support performance. An optimizer scores drafts against target keywords, and reports track traffic and engagement across channels. AI features help generate outlines and drafts, rewrite content, and adapt posts for social networks, and a library of integrations connects WordPress, HubSpot, and other tools. It’s popular with agencies that manage multiple clients, and with in-house teams.

item.title: Wealth.com
item.description:
Wealth.com brings estate planning into the advisory relationship. Advisors can generate estate documents for clients through guided workflows, with attorney review options, and offer a client portal that shows the plan visually. A vault stores documents.

AI reads existing estate documents and summarizes provisions, beneficiaries, and issues, which helps advisors understand a client’s situation quickly. The platform integrates with financial planning tools so estate information sits alongside the rest of the plan.

item.title: Whistle
item.description:
Whistle sold small GPS devices that attached to a pet’s collar and reported location through cellular networks. Owners could set safe zones, get an alert when a pet left them, and view recent routes. The devices also tracked activity, rest, and behaviors such as scratching and licking, and the app compared these against typical patterns to point out possible health changes.

The company was owned by Mars Petcare before Tractive, an Austrian pet tracking company, took over the brand. Rather than run two competing platforms, Tractive shut down the Whistle service, and the trackers no longer work. Tractive offered affected customers a replacement device, so owners are generally pointed to its products.

item.title: Whoop
item.description: WHOOP is a screenless wearable worn on the wrist or in apparel. It records heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, blood oxygen, and movement around the clock, and its app turns that into daily scores for recovery, strain, and sleep. The idea is to show how prepared your body is to train hard or rest, and to give athletes and health-conscious people a sense of how habits like alcohol or late nights affect them.

item.title: 6sense
item.description:
6sense helps B2B teams find buyers who are not yet raising their hands. It collects signals from many sources, such as web visits, content consumption, and third-party research activity, identifies the companies behind the anonymous traffic, and uses machine learning to predict which accounts are in the market and at what stage of the buying journey. Teams see lists of target accounts ranked by readiness to buy.

The platform acts on those insights. Marketing can run advertising aimed at accounts showing interest, sales gets alerts when key accounts spike in activity, and workflows enroll contacts in email sequences. AI agents help with outreach and qualification, and integrations with CRMs and marketing automation tools keep data in sync. Predictions rely on data from many sources, so they are probabilistic.

item.title: ADP
item.description:
ADP is one of the best-known payroll companies in the world. It pays employees, files payroll taxes, and manages benefits administration, time and attendance, hiring, and HR records. Products range from simple small-business payroll to large, multi-country platforms for enterprises, and many companies outsource payroll entirely to ADP to ensure accuracy and compliance with changing tax rules.

Technology is increasingly part of the offering. ADP uses AI for assistants that answer HR and payroll questions, flag errors before payroll runs, and give managers insight into workforce trends, using its large dataset of payroll information to benchmark pay and turnover. The platform integrates with accounting and HR systems, and mobile apps let employees see pay stubs and request time off.

item.title: Ahrefs
item.description: Ahrefs is best known for its backlink data. Its crawler maps links across the web, so you can look at any site and see who links to it, which pages draw the most traffic, and what keywords bring visitors. Site Explorer is the tool most people open first, and it is often used to study a competitor’s strategy. Keywords Explorer suggests search terms and estimates how hard each one would be to rank for.

item.title: Airbyte
item.description: Airbyte solves the data movement problem. Data teams use it to pull information from applications, databases, and APIs, such as Salesforce, Postgres, Stripe, and Google Ads, and load it into destinations such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks, on a schedule. Hundreds of pre-built connectors cover common sources, and a low-code builder, with AI assistance, lets teams create connectors for others. Because it is open source, the connector catalog grows with community contributions.

item.title: AlphaSense
item.description: AlphaSense is a search engine for business information. Analysts, investors, and strategy teams use it to find what companies and experts are saying across a large body of documents: earnings call transcripts, SEC filings, broker and industry research, press releases, news, and expert call transcripts. Its search understands financial language, so a query for supply chain risk or pricing pressure returns relevant passages instead of just keyword matches, with highlights and context.

item.title: Amplitude AI
item.description: Amplitude helps product teams see what users actually do. You instrument your app or website to send events, such as signing up, clicking a button, or finishing a purchase, and Amplitude turns them into funnels, retention curves, user paths, and cohorts. These views answer questions like where new users drop off and which features bring people back. It is used by product managers, designers, and data analysts at companies from startups to large enterprises.

item.title: Attention Insight
item.description: Attention Insight offers an inexpensive shortcut to a classic design question: will anyone notice this? Upload a screenshot, ad, packaging mockup, or video, and its AI produces a heatmap of the areas likely to draw the eye in the first few seconds. The model is trained on eye-tracking data, so the predictions approximate what real viewers would do. It returns results in seconds, which makes it practical to compare several versions of a design.

item.title: Balto
item.description:
Balto sits beside an agent during a call. The software listens to the conversation, recognizes where it is in a script or process, and shows prompts on the agent’s screen: a question to ask, a compliance statement to read, a way to answer an objection. The aim is consistent performance across a team and less reliance on memory.

Supervisors benefit as well. Balto scores calls automatically, shows which behaviors lead to better outcomes, and reduces the number of calls reviewers must listen to by hand. New agents can ramp faster because the software coaches them in real time. Industries with strict rules, such as insurance and financial services, use it for compliance.

item.title: Betterworks
item.description:
Betterworks supports how companies manage performance throughout the year. Employees set goals or OKRs that link to company priorities, managers hold regular check-ins, and feedback and recognition are captured along the way. Review cycles then draw on this record, so evaluations rely less on recent memory.

AI features help with the writing and analysis. An assistant can improve goal statements, summarize a year of feedback into review drafts, and suggest coaching points, while analytics show goal progress and engagement across teams. Integrations connect with HR systems like Workday and collaboration tools such as Slack and Microsoft Teams.

item.title: BILL AI
item.description:
BILL helps businesses handle bills and payments without paper and manual entry. Vendors’ invoices arrive by email or upload, the system extracts the details, routes them for approval, and schedules payment by ACH, check, or card. On the receivables side, it sends invoices to customers and collects payments.

AI takes on the data entry. It reads invoice fields, suggests accounting categories, matches invoices to purchase orders and receipts, and flags duplicates or unusual items. Integrations with QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, and other accounting systems keep the books in sync, and spend management tools add corporate cards and expense tracking.

item.title: Botkeeper
item.description:
Botkeeper offered accounting firms a way to scale bookkeeping with automation. Its software connected to clients’ accounting systems, categorized transactions with machine learning, reconciled accounts, and prepared financial statements, with human reviewers checking the work. The aim was to let firms serve more clients with the same staff and to reduce routine data entry.

The company raised substantial funding, but it shut down after losing a large share of its revenue when major customers were acquired and changed their arrangements. It then sold its Infinite AI platform to Xendoo, a bookkeeping firm, which said it would keep the platform active and supported as its own division. The long-term roadmap is less clear, and customers had to decide whether to move.

item.title: Brandwatch
item.description:
Brandwatch is used by marketing, communications, and research teams to understand what people say online. It collects posts and mentions from social networks, news sites, forums, blogs, and reviews, and lets analysts build searches to track a brand, a competitor, a campaign, or a topic. Dashboards show volume over time, sentiment, demographics, top influencers, and emerging themes, which helps with campaign measurement, crisis monitoring, and product feedback.

AI plays a role in making sense of the data. Language models classify sentiment and topics, group conversations into themes, summarize large sets of posts, and answer questions about the findings in natural language. Image recognition finds logos in pictures posted without any text. Alerts warn teams when mentions spike, and the social management side supports publishing and responding to messages from one place.

item.title: Buffer
item.description: Buffer is built for people who want to run their social accounts without living in each app. You connect your profiles, write a post once, adjust it per platform, and schedule it into a queue that publishes at set times. A calendar view shows what is planned, and an idea library keeps drafts and inspiration in one place. The interface is deliberately plain, which is a big part of why freelancers, creators, and small businesses like it.

item.title: Buzzsprout
item.description:
Buzzsprout focuses on being the easiest way to get a podcast online. You upload an audio file, add show notes, and publish, and it distributes the episode to Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other directories through an RSS feed it manages. It provides an embeddable player for your website, detailed download statistics, and tools for promoting episodes on social media.

Additional features help creators improve and grow. Magic Mastering automatically cleans up and balances audio loudness, an AI transcription service creates transcripts, and tools can generate chapters, episode titles, and descriptions. Dynamic content features and a way to import an existing podcast make switching easy. Monetization options include support from listeners and ads in some plans.

item.title: Carbon Trust
item.description:
The Carbon Trust began as a UK organization set up to help businesses and the public sector cut emissions, and it now works internationally. It advises companies on how to measure their greenhouse gas emissions across operations and supply chains, set reduction targets, and plan the changes needed to meet them. Its work spans corporate carbon footprinting, product footprints, net zero strategy, and support with climate disclosure requirements.

A well-known part of its business is certification and standards. The Carbon Trust Standard recognizes organizations that measure and reduce their footprint, and other programs verify claims about products and supply chains. Software and data tools support these services, and AI is used to process large amounts of supplier and energy data, estimate emissions where measured data is missing, and identify the best reduction opportunities.

item.title: Causal
item.description:
Causal was created for finance teams that outgrew spreadsheets. Users build models from blocks that represent revenue, headcount, and costs, link them to data from accounting and CRM systems, and see results as charts and dashboards. The structure makes models easier to follow and share than a sprawling workbook.

Scenario planning is a core strength. Teams can change assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing, and compare outcomes side by side, then present the results to executives and investors. AI features help create models from descriptions and explain changes in numbers.

item.title: CB Insights
item.description:
CB Insights tracks the innovation economy. Its database covers private companies, funding rounds, investors, acquisitions, patents, and news, and analysts and algorithms turn that into research on market trends. Corporate strategy teams, investors, and consultants use it to understand which sectors are growing and who the major players are.

Features include company profiles, market maps, forecasts of company outcomes, and an AI assistant that answers questions from the platform’s data and research. Alerts and newsletters keep subscribers up to date, and tools support building lists of companies matching specific criteria.

item.title: ClimaCell
item.description:
Tomorrow.io focuses on weather as a business input. Companies in aviation, logistics, energy, retail, and sports use its platform to get forecasts and alerts tailored to their locations and operations, such as a warning when wind will halt crane operations or when snow will affect deliveries. The goal is to turn weather into decisions, not just data.

It builds its own data sources. The company has launched satellites carrying radar to observe precipitation, which supplements ground sensors and models and helps in regions with limited coverage. AI blends these inputs to make short-range forecasts, and an assistant helps users create alerts and ask questions about conditions. APIs deliver the data into other applications.

item.title: Climate FieldView
item.description:
Climate FieldView helps farmers use their data. With a device plugged into farm equipment, FieldView Drive collects information about planting, applications, and harvest, and the data syncs to the cloud, where farmers view maps of their fields, compare hybrids and practices, and analyze yield. Satellite imagery tracks crop health during the season, and weather data and field notes add context.

Advanced features support planning. Variable-rate prescriptions tell equipment to apply seed and fertilizer at different rates across a field based on zones, which can improve efficiency, and scripts or models estimate the profitability of decisions. Integrations with equipment and other agriculture software reduce manual data transfers. Machine learning supports yield predictions and recommendations.

item.title: ContentStudio
item.description:
ContentStudio combines content discovery, creation, and publishing. Users find trending topics and articles, curate and share them, write posts with an AI assistant, and schedule to networks such as Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, and WordPress blogs. A calendar shows what is planned across channels.

Features for teams and agencies include approval workflows, client management, white-label reports, and analytics on performance. The AI writer generates captions, hashtags, and blog drafts, and image tools help create visuals. Social inbox features centralize replies and comments.

item.title: Crimson Hexagon
item.description: Crimson Hexagon was a consumer insights company that analyzed social media, news, forums, and review data at large scale. It was known for its ForSight platform and for machine learning that classified posts by sentiment and topic with accuracy that researchers could tune. Market researchers, agencies, and brands used it to track what people said about products and campaigns, and its archive of historical social data was a draw for studying trends over time.

item.title: Crunchbase
item.description:
Crunchbase is a widely used database about startups and private companies. Users look up a company to see its founders, funding history, investors, and news, or search for companies by industry, location, and stage. Investors, salespeople, and researchers use it to find targets and track activity.

Predictive features add forward-looking signals. AI models estimate which companies are likely to raise money, grow, or be acquired, and alerts notify users when relevant events happen. Lists and integrations send data into CRMs for prospecting.

item.title: Culture Amp
item.description:
Culture Amp helps companies listen to employees. HR teams run engagement, onboarding, and exit surveys, analyze the results by team and demographic group, and compare against benchmarks from other organizations. Dashboards point out areas where scores are low and what drives them.

The platform also covers performance and development, with review cycles, goal tracking, and feedback. AI helps by summarizing open-ended comments into themes, drafting review text, and recommending actions to managers, which saves analysts days of reading. An assistant answers questions about results.

item.title: DataRobot
item.description:
DataRobot pioneered automated machine learning. A data team uploads a dataset, and the platform tries many algorithms and feature combinations, ranks them, and explains the best models, which lowers the barrier to building predictive models for tasks such as churn, demand, and risk. It also handles deployment and monitoring, tracking model accuracy and drift once models are live.

The company has pivoted toward generative AI and agents. Its platform now helps companies build and run AI agents and applications, with governance features such as documentation, bias checks, approvals, and audit trails that matter in industries such as banking, insurance, and healthcare. It can run in the cloud or on a company’s own infrastructure and integrates with major cloud providers and data platforms.

item.title: dbt Cloud
item.description:
dbt, short for data build tool, became the standard way to transform raw data inside a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Analysts write SQL select statements, define dependencies among them, and dbt builds tables and views in the right order, with version control, testing, and documentation. This brings software engineering practices like code review and continuous integration to analytics work.

dbt Cloud is the hosted product from dbt Labs. It provides a browser-based IDE, job scheduling, CI that tests changes before they reach production, a data catalog with lineage, and a semantic layer that defines metrics once for use across BI tools. AI features help generate models, tests, and documentation, and answer questions about the project, which speeds up repetitive tasks.

item.title: Dimensions
item.description:
Dimensions connects different kinds of research outputs. Instead of searching only for papers, users can see how a grant led to publications, which patents cite a study, and whether a trial or policy document refers to it. The linked structure helps trace the path from funding to impact.

Institutions, funders, and researchers use it for several purposes. Universities benchmark their output, funders track results of the grants they award, and companies look for experts and emerging fields. AI features summarize results, help with literature searches, and surface connections, and APIs let organizations pull data into their own systems.

item.title: Domo AI
item.description:
Domo aims to put an organization’s data in one place. It connects to hundreds of sources, from databases and spreadsheets to marketing and finance platforms, and lets users clean and combine data and then build dashboards and reports. Business users can view metrics on the web or mobile and set alerts, and developers can build custom apps on top of the data.

AI is built through the product. Users can ask questions in natural language and receive charts and answers, models can forecast and detect anomalies, and AI agents and workflows can automate tasks, such as summarizing reports or triggering actions when numbers change. Domo also lets companies connect their own models, and offers governance features for data access.

item.title: Dovetail
item.description:
Dovetail gives research teams a home for customer feedback. Researchers upload interviews and other data, and the platform transcribes recordings, lets them highlight key quotes, and organizes everything so insights can be found later. Teams build a searchable repository instead of losing findings in slide decks.

AI shortens the analysis step. It tags content automatically, groups related feedback into themes, summarizes sessions, and answers questions across a body of research. Reports and shareable highlights help researchers communicate with product teams and executives, and integrations pull in data from support and survey tools.

item.title: Elicit
item.description:
Elicit helps researchers move through academic literature faster. A user asks a research question, and Elicit searches a large database of papers, presents relevant results, and extracts details such as sample size, methods, and outcomes into a table. Seeing structured comparisons across studies is much quicker than reading each paper in full.

Additional tools support systematic review work. Users can screen papers against criteria, summarize findings, and build reports, with citations tied to the passages in each paper so claims can be checked. It is used by students, academics, and professionals in evidence-based fields.

item.title: Expensify
item.description:
Expensify is known for making expense reports less painful. Employees photograph receipts or forward them by email, SmartScan extracts the merchant, date, and amount, and the app builds a report for submission. Managers approve in the app, and approved expenses sync to accounting software.

Other features cover company spending. The Expensify Card gives employees corporate cards with real-time receipts matching, policies flag out-of-bounds expenses automatically, and mileage tracking and per diems handle travel. AI helps categorize spending and spot policy issues.

item.title: Explainpaper
item.description: Explainpaper targets a familiar frustration: academic papers are dense and full of jargon. You upload a PDF, select the sentence, equation, or paragraph you do not understand, and the tool gives a plain-language explanation. You can adjust the level, from a lay audience to an expert, and ask follow-up questions about the paper. It was popular with students and curious readers who wanted to follow a paper outside their own field.

item.title: Fivetran
item.description:
Fivetran handles the extract and load steps of data pipelines. A team connects sources such as SaaS applications, databases, and files, picks a destination warehouse, and Fivetran keeps the data synced, adapting automatically when source schemas change. This saves engineers from building and maintaining custom connectors.

The company merged with dbt Labs, the maker of the popular transformation tool, bringing loading and transformation together under one roof. Related products include a metadata and governance layer, and tools that prepare data for AI agents. Features for monitoring, anomaly detection, and lineage help teams trust their data.

item.title: Flick AI
item.description:
Flick targets people who manage social media without a large team. It combines content planning with AI writing: you can brainstorm ideas, generate captions and post drafts in your own style, and organize them on a calendar before scheduling. A hashtag tool suggests relevant tags, and an analytics view helps you see what performs well.

An AI assistant trained on your past content tries to match your tone and topics, so drafts need less editing than generic output. The platform supports multiple networks, including Instagram, LinkedIn, and TikTok, and offers collaboration features for agencies or small teams to review and approve content. Prompts and templates help with common formats such as carousels and short videos.

item.title: Foursquare
item.description:
Foursquare began as an app for checking in at places and discovering venues, but its main business today is location data. The company maintains a large database of points of interest, including businesses, landmarks, and venues, with details like categories, hours, and popularity. Developers use its Places API to add search, recommendations, and place information to maps and apps, and brands use its data to understand where people go.

Beyond place data, Foursquare provides tools for analyzing movement and location behavior. Panels of opted-in users allow measurement of foot traffic to stores, audience analysis, and attribution for advertising, and mapping and geospatial products let companies visualize and process location data at scale. Machine learning keeps place information up to date and helps match records from different sources.

item.title: Frase
item.description:
Frase helps content teams plan and write articles that can rank. Enter a keyword, and Frase analyzes the top search results to show the topics, questions, and headings they cover and the terms they use, then creates a brief that guides a writer. As you draft, a score shows how well your article covers the topic compared with competitors, and suggestions help fill gaps.

AI features support writing and optimization. Frase can generate outlines and drafts, answer questions drawn from search data, and update existing articles to improve their performance. Newer tools track visibility in AI-generated answers from assistants and search engines, reflecting the shift in how people find information, and an agent can handle parts of the content workflow. Integrations with Google Search Console and publishing tools connect data to action.

item.title: Granular
item.description:
Granular was built to help large farm operations plan and track their business. Its software covered field activity and agronomy, inventory, labor, equipment, and financial reporting, and tried to give farm managers a view of costs and profitability for each crop and field. Corteva Agriscience acquired it, and for several years it was marketed to commercial growers who wanted enterprise-level tools.

The product line has since been restructured. Corteva discontinued Granular Agronomy, the field-level software, and sold the financial and business-management side to a company called Traction Ag. The pieces now go by different names and are maintained by different companies, which makes it important to confirm what is currently offered under the Granular name.

item.title: Greenhouse
item.description: Greenhouse is an applicant tracking system for companies that want hiring to be systematic instead of ad hoc. Each job has a defined process: a posting, a set of stages, interview kits with questions, and scorecards that interviewers fill out against the same criteria. The aim is to reduce bias and gut-feel decisions by making every candidate go through the same structured steps. Recruiters, hiring managers, and interviewers each get a view suited to their part of the work.

item.title: GrowthBar
item.description:
GrowthBar tries to simplify SEO for people who are not specialists. You enter a keyword, and the tool shows search volume and difficulty, related keywords, and what the top-ranking pages cover, including their headings and word counts. A Chrome extension displays similar data directly in search results, which helps when researching competitors.

The AI content features turn that research into drafts. GrowthBar can generate outlines, blog posts, and meta descriptions, and tools for rewriting and expanding text help refine them. It also includes rank tracking and backlink data, and an AI assistant to help brainstorm topics. The target users are small business owners, freelancers, and agencies that publish content regularly.

item.title: H2O.ai
item.description:
H2O.ai built its reputation on open-source machine learning. H2O-3 is a widely used library for training models on large datasets, with an AutoML feature that tries many algorithms and picks the best. The company’s commercial Driverless AI automated feature engineering and model building for business users, and its tools have been used in finance, insurance, and healthcare.

More recently, H2O.ai has focused on generative AI. H2O LLM Studio lets teams fine-tune language models without much code, h2oGPT is an open-source project for chatting with documents, and its enterprise platform lets companies deploy private assistants and agents, including on-premises or in air-gapped environments. It has also released small language models designed to run efficiently.

item.title: HiBob
item.description:
HiBob is built for companies that want a modern HR system for distributed teams. It stores employee records, handles onboarding and time off, supports performance reviews, and manages compensation and benefits. The interface is designed for employees as well as HR, with a social feel and company-wide features.

Analytics and AI help leaders. Compensation benchmarking compares pay with market data, workforce planning tools model headcount, and an assistant answers HR questions and drafts documents. Payroll integrations and a marketplace of apps connect Bob with finance and IT systems.

item.title: Hootsuite
item.description:
Hootsuite is one of the oldest social media management tools. Teams connect accounts for networks such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, TikTok, and YouTube, plan content on a calendar, schedule posts, and respond to comments and messages in a shared inbox. Approval workflows suit larger organizations.

Listening and analytics tools track brand mentions and compare performance across channels. OwlyWriter, the AI assistant, helps write captions, suggest ideas, and repurpose content. Advertising management and employee advocacy products extend the suite for enterprises.

item.title: Hotjar AI
item.description:
Hotjar helps teams see what visitors actually do on a site. Heatmaps show where people click, move, and scroll, session recordings replay individual visits, and on-page surveys and feedback widgets ask visitors what they think. Together they reveal confusing layouts, broken elements, and places where people give up, which complements numbers from analytics tools that show what happened but not why.

AI cuts down the time it takes to find insights. Instead of watching hundreds of recordings, teams can get automatic summaries of sessions, highlights of common frustrations, and analysis of open-ended survey responses grouped into themes. This helps designers, product managers, and marketers decide what to fix first. Funnels and trends let you see where users drop out, and integrations send findings to tools like Slack, Jira, and HubSpot.

item.title: Inciteful
item.description:
Inciteful takes a paper or a list of papers and builds a network of the research that surrounds them. Using citation data, it identifies the papers that are most connected, which tend to be foundational works, review articles, and recent developments. You enter a DOI, title, or several seed papers, and the tool shows a ranked list of papers, authors, and journals, with visual graphs of how they connect.

It is most useful early in a literature review. Starting from a few papers you know, you can discover similar and influential work you might have missed, track the most cited authors in the area, and spot new papers that cite your seeds. A Paper Discovery view finds the most important papers connected to your starting point, and a Literature Connector finds papers that link two different topics. Results can be exported to reference managers.

item.title: Kensho
item.description:
Kensho began as a startup applying machine learning to financial markets and was acquired by S&P Global, where it operates as the company’s AI innovation hub. Its products address practical data problems in finance. Kensho Link matches records between data sets, such as linking company names across different sources, Kensho Classify tags documents by category, and Kensho Extract pulls data out of PDFs and filings.

More recent work connects financial data to generative AI. Kensho develops tools that allow AI assistants and agents to access S&P Global’s data reliably, with grounding that provides sources for answers, plus language models and benchmarks for finance. Its technology supports S&P products and is available to clients who want to build their own applications.

item.title: Klaviyo AI
item.description:
Klaviyo is built on the idea that a store’s own customer data is the best basis for marketing. It connects to platforms like Shopify, BigCommerce, and WooCommerce, pulling in orders, browsing behavior, and product information. Marketers build segments, such as customers who bought twice in the last 60 days, and send targeted email and SMS campaigns and automated flows, like abandoned cart reminders, welcome series, and post-purchase follow-ups.

AI adds prediction and automation. Klaviyo estimates a customer’s likelihood to buy again, expected lifetime value, and probable next order date, and uses those signals for segmentation. Product recommendations personalize emails, send-time optimization chooses delivery times, and generative tools write subject lines and campaign copy and build flows from a description. A customer hub, reviews, and a CDP add other parts of the retention workflow.

item.title: Later
item.description:
Later started as a way to plan Instagram feeds visually. Users drag photos and videos onto a calendar, see how the grid will look, write captions, and schedule posts to go out automatically. It has since expanded to other networks, including TikTok, Pinterest, LinkedIn, Facebook, and X, with tools to manage a content library, collaborate with teammates, and track results.

Other features support social growth. A link-in-bio page lets creators send followers to multiple destinations, analytics show which posts perform best and when audiences are most active, and AI helps write captions, suggest hashtags, and repurpose content. The company also owns an influencer marketing platform, which helps brands find creators and manage campaigns.

item.title: Lens.org
item.description:
The Lens aims to make innovation data open. It combines a very large database of patents from patent offices worldwide with scholarly works from sources like Crossref, PubMed, and others. Users can search by keywords, inventors, institutions, or classifications, and the results show patent families, legal status, citations, and links to the full text where available. The free access sets it apart from commercial patent databases.

The key feature is the connection between patents and papers. It tracks which scholarly works are cited in patents, which lets researchers and technology transfer offices see how academic research is used in inventions, and lets innovators find prior art. Collections let you save and share sets of results, and analytics and dashboards visualize trends, such as top applicants or fast-growing technology areas. Sequence search supports biotechnology patents.

item.title: Llamasoft
item.description:
Llamasoft helped companies answer strategic supply chain questions. Where should factories and warehouses be placed? How would costs change if a port closes or demand shifts? Its software builds a digital model of a supply network, then uses optimization and simulation to test alternatives and recommend the best configuration, balancing cost, service levels, and risk. Large manufacturers, retailers, and consumer goods companies used it for network design and planning.

Coupa acquired Llamasoft and folded it into its business spend management platform, so customers can connect supply chain decisions with procurement and spend data. The technology continues under Coupa branding, with capabilities such as network optimization, inventory and sourcing analysis, and demand sensing, supported by machine learning and a digital twin of the supply chain.

item.title: Maze
item.description:
Maze helps product teams learn from users. Designers import a prototype from Figma, set tasks for participants, and share a link to run a test that records clicks, paths, and success rates. Surveys, card sorts, and interview studies are supported as well, and a panel service can recruit participants.

AI speeds up analysis. It transcribes sessions, pulls out themes and quotes, and writes summaries of what the data shows, so teams spend less time sorting through recordings. Reports can be shared with stakeholders.

item.title: Metabase
item.description:
Metabase makes data approachable. Connected to a database or warehouse, it lets non-technical users build questions by clicking through filters and summaries, view results as charts, and assemble dashboards. Analysts can write SQL when they need it, and everything is shareable.

The AI assistant lets users describe what they want, and generates the query or chart, which helps people who do not know the data model. Embedded analytics lets companies place dashboards in their own products. Permissions and models keep data governed.

item.title: Metricool
item.description:
Metricool brings several marketing tasks into one dashboard. Users can plan and schedule posts across networks on a calendar, see analytics on posts, followers, and competitors, and manage Facebook, Instagram, Google, and TikTok ads reports. A link-in-bio tool, inbox for comments and messages, and web analytics help connect social activity to site traffic.

Reporting is a strong point. Customizable reports can be exported or scheduled for clients, and integrations connect with Looker Studio and other business intelligence tools, which suits agencies. AI features help write captions, suggest posting times, and generate content ideas, and a feature can plan a calendar from a brief. Plans cover multiple brands, so one account can manage several clients.

item.title: Missinglettr
item.description:
Missinglettr automates a task many content creators neglect: promoting their articles over time. You connect your blog or paste a link, and the tool analyzes the post to pull out quotes, statistics, and highlights. It then generates a series of social posts, with images, scheduled across weeks and months, so a single article continues to attract visitors long after it’s published.

Other features round out the platform. A curation tool suggests relevant content from other sources to share, a social media scheduler handles regular posting, and analytics show engagement. Collaboration features allow agencies and teams to manage several brands. AI helps with writing captions and variations, and automated hashtag suggestions save time.

item.title: Monday.com
item.description:
Monday.com organizes work in colorful boards that resemble spreadsheets. Teams track projects, sales pipelines, marketing campaigns, and operations with columns for status, owners, dates, and more, and view the same data as a timeline, calendar, or chart. No-code automations handle routine updates and notifications.

The platform has expanded into products for sales CRM, service desks, and software development, built on the same foundation. AI assistants create boards from a description, summarize items and updates, write content, and extract information, and agents can take on tasks within workflows.

item.title: Morningstar AI
item.description:
Morningstar is known for independent research on funds, stocks, and markets. Its star ratings for mutual funds and ETFs became a standard reference, and analysts publish research and fair value estimates on companies. Individual investors use its website and premium subscriptions to screen investments and build portfolios, while advisors and institutions use products like Morningstar Direct for deeper analysis, portfolio construction, and reporting.

AI has been added to make research easier to navigate. Mo is a conversational assistant that answers investing questions using Morningstar’s research and data, summarizes reports, and explains concepts, with an emphasis on drawing from the company’s own vetted content to limit errors. Other uses include automated summaries of earnings calls and analyst notes, and data tools that help build screens and analyze holdings.

item.title: Mosaic
item.description:
Mosaic is aimed at finance teams that want a modern view of the business. It pulls data from accounting systems, sales tools, and HR platforms into a single model, so metrics like revenue, headcount, and cash are current and consistent. Teams build reports and board decks from live data.

Forecasting and scenario tools let teams test assumptions, such as hiring plans or pricing changes, and see the impact. AI allows users to ask questions in plain language and get analysis, and automates routine commentary and variance explanations.

item.title: Moz Pro
item.description:
Moz was one of the earliest SEO software companies, and Moz Pro remains a staple for agencies and in-house marketers. Users research keywords, audit sites for technical problems, track rankings over time, and analyze links, with Domain Authority, Moz’s well-known score, used as a quick measure of a site’s strength.

The MozBar browser extension overlays metrics on search results and web pages, making competitor checks quick. Reporting tools produce client-ready summaries, and newer AI features suggest priorities and help with content. A separate local product manages business listings.

item.title: NeuralText
item.description:
NeuralText is an SEO content suite. Users find keywords, group them into clusters by intent, study what ranks for a term, and create content briefs that list topics and questions to cover. The AI writer then drafts articles or sections using those guidelines.

The tool aims to let one person handle research, planning, and drafting. A content editor scores text against the brief, and additional templates cover ads, product descriptions, and social posts.

item.title: NotebookLM Plus
item.description: NotebookLM Plus gives heavier users more room in NotebookLM, Google’s tool for working with your own documents. The free version lets you add sources, ask questions with citations, and generate study aids, but it limits the number of notebooks, sources, and daily queries. The Plus tier lifts those limits, so people with large projects, such as researchers, students writing theses, or analysts working across many documents, can keep more material in one place.

item.title: Okendo
item.description:
Okendo helps online stores build trust with reviews. After a purchase, it asks customers for reviews with photos and video, displays them on product pages, and syndicates them to Google. Surveys and attributes gather more detail about the customer and product fit.

Additional tools include a loyalty and referral program and a customer data layer. AI summarizes reviews into themes, analyzes sentiment, and suggests replies, helping merchants learn what customers like and dislike. Integrations connect with email, helpdesk, and ads tools.

item.title: OpenRead
item.description:
OpenRead is built for people who read a lot of research. After you import a paper, an AI assistant can answer questions about it, explain terms, summarize sections, and pull out items like methods, results, and limitations. A structured summary view lays out the main points in a consistent format, which helps when scanning many papers for a review.

The platform extends beyond a single paper. It helps search the literature, organize papers into collections, take notes alongside the text, and generate outlines or review drafts from selected sources. Support for multiple languages makes it useful for researchers who read in a second language, and translation features help with papers published in other languages.

item.title: Paper Digest
item.description:
Paper Digest helps researchers keep up with a flood of new papers. Instead of scanning listings of new submissions every day, a user sets up topics or keywords and gets a personalized digest with short AI-generated summaries of matching papers. This helps researchers spot relevant work quickly and decide which papers merit a full read.

The service also publishes curated summaries of papers from major conferences and journals, and offers a platform to search, summarize, and organize papers. Paper Digest builds on text summarization models to produce abstracts and key points, and it provides tools such as a reader and a way to generate a quick literature overview. Some features are open to everyone, while others sit behind a login or subscription.

item.title: Perplexity
item.description: For research, Perplexity is useful because it shows its sources. Each answer comes with numbered citations to the pages it used, so you can open the link and check a claim before relying on it. You can narrow searches to particular kinds of sources, such as academic papers, and keep asking follow-up questions that build on the earlier ones. This makes it a quicker starting point than a list of search results for questions that need several sources.

item.title: Perplexity Labs
item.description: Labs goes beyond answering a question. You describe a project, such as a market analysis, a financial model, or a small dashboard, and Labs works for several minutes, combining web research, code execution, and chart creation. It then returns finished assets: a written report, a spreadsheet, charts, or a simple web app that you can download or share. The tool uses a team of specialized steps behind the scenes, so the output is more like a deliverable than a chat reply.

item.title: Perplexity Pages
item.description:
Pages is a publishing layer on top of Perplexity’s research. After you explore a topic with the assistant, you can convert the thread into a structured page with headings, summaries, and citations to the sources it used. It organizes the material in the way a short article or study guide would be written, instead of leaving you with a conversation log.

You control the result. Sections can be rewritten, reordered, or removed, images can be added, and the page can be published with a shareable link or kept private. Educators use Pages to create study guides, students for report drafts, and professionals for quick explainers on topics they research often. Because the citations travel with the content, readers can check where claims came from.

item.title: Personetics
item.description:
Personetics supplies the intelligence behind money management features in banking apps. Banks connect transaction data, and the platform generates timely, personalized messages and suggestions, like warning a customer that a bill will overdraw their account or noticing a good time to save.

The aim is a more engaging and useful banking relationship. Personetics works with large banks around the world and presents itself as a way to turn data into proactive guidance. AI generates the insights and chooses when and how to show them.

item.title: Pilot
item.description:
Pilot offers accounting as a service. A company connects its bank accounts and tools, and Pilot’s team and software keep the books, close each month, prepare financial statements, and handle tax filings. Clients get a dedicated bookkeeper and a dashboard.

Automation takes on the repetitive work, such as categorizing transactions, while humans check results and answer questions. Add-on services include CFO advice, R&D tax credits, and sales tax support.

Pilot is priced by monthly fee based on complexity, and aimed at startups and small to mid-sized businesses. It is a service, not self-serve software. Alternatives include Bench (which shut down and was acquired by Employer.com), Puzzle, Digits, Xero with an accountant, and QuickBooks Live. Pilot suits startups that want outsourced accounting.

item.title: PitchBook
item.description:
PitchBook tracks private markets. Its database covers companies, funding rounds, investors, funds, acquisitions, and valuations, and analysts use it to find targets, benchmark deals, and research sectors. Reports and data feeds support investment decisions and strategy work.

AI tools help users query the database in natural language, summarize companies and markets, and speed up research tasks. Integrations with Excel and CRM systems bring data into daily workflows. The company also publishes market research.

item.title: Plaid
item.description: Plaid connects apps to bank accounts. When you link an account in a budgeting app, investment platform, or payments service, Plaid’s interface asks you to sign in to your bank, and the app then receives only the data you permit. Developers use Plaid’s APIs to verify account ownership, check balances, read transaction history, confirm identity, assess income and assets for lending, and initiate transfers, without building separate integrations with thousands of banks.

item.title: Planet Labs
item.description: Planet Labs built its business on frequency. Rather than a few large satellites, it operates a large number of small ones, so it can photograph almost every part of the land surface regularly. That consistency allows users to watch change over time: crops growing, forests being cleared, ice melting, construction progressing, or ships moving. The imagery has a lower resolution than the sharpest commercial satellites but far greater frequency, and some higher-resolution satellites supplement it.

item.title: PostHog AI
item.description:
PostHog bundles the tools product teams use to understand and improve their software. After adding its SDK, you can track events, build funnels and retention charts, watch session recordings, run experiments, release features gradually with flags, collect feedback through surveys, and analyze data with SQL. Having these in one product, with a shared data set, avoids the cost and complexity of stitching several tools together.

AI features include an assistant that can answer questions about your data, write queries, create charts, and summarize insights in plain language, and tools for monitoring AI applications such as tracing model calls and costs. Because PostHog is open source, it can be self-hosted for data control, or used through PostHog Cloud, and a pipeline can send data to other destinations.

item.title: Power BI
item.description: Power BI turns raw data into visual reports. You connect to sources such as Excel files, SQL databases, cloud services, and Microsoft Fabric, shape the data, define relationships and calculations, and build dashboards with charts, maps, and slicers. Reports can be published to the Power BI service, shared with colleagues, refreshed on a schedule, and embedded in other applications. Because it fits neatly with Excel, Teams, SharePoint, and Azure, it is the default BI tool for many Microsoft-centered companies.

item.title: Qwilr
item.description:
Qwilr replaces static PDF proposals with web pages. A seller builds a proposal from blocks, such as text, images, videos, pricing tables, and acceptance sections, and sends a link. Buyers can adjust options in a pricing table, and sign online, which shortens the path to closing.

Analytics show who viewed the page, how long they spent on each section, and when they came back, which guides follow-up. Templates keep branding consistent, and integrations push data into CRMs. AI drafts content from notes and suggests improvements.

item.title: Retool AI
item.description:
Retool is designed for engineers who need to build internal software quickly. Developers connect databases, APIs, and services, drag components such as tables, forms, and charts onto a canvas, and write queries and logic in SQL and JavaScript where needed. The result is an application for operations, support, or finance teams to manage data, approve requests, or run workflows, built in hours instead of weeks.

AI is integrated across the platform. A generative assistant can create an app from a description, write queries, and generate components, and Retool offers AI actions to classify, summarize, and extract information as parts of apps and workflows. Retool Agents let teams build agents that use their data and tools, and workflows automate scheduled and event-driven tasks. Enterprise controls cover permissions, audit logs, and self-hosting.

item.title: Rippling
item.description:
Rippling combines employee data with the systems that depend on it. When a person joins, Rippling creates their payroll record, sets up benefits, provisions laptops and software accounts, and orders equipment, using one source of truth. Changes in the employee record cascade across the systems.

Modules cover HR, payroll in many countries, time and attendance, benefits, device and app management, and corporate cards and expenses. A workflow engine lets admins automate approvals and tasks, and AI assistants answer questions and draft content.

item.title: Roboflow
item.description:
Roboflow helps teams build computer vision applications without starting from scratch. You upload images or video, label objects with AI-assisted annotation tools, and Roboflow handles formatting, augmentation, and splitting data into training sets. It then trains or fine-tunes models such as YOLO and other popular architectures, and shows performance metrics so you can see where the model fails and what data to add.

Deployment is a main focus. Models can run through a hosted API, on your own servers, or at the edge on devices such as NVIDIA Jetson or a mobile phone. Workflows let you chain models with logic and actions, for example detecting a defect, counting items, and sending an alert to a system. Roboflow Universe is a public collection of datasets and pretrained models shared by the community, which gives a fast start for common tasks.

item.title: Salesforce Einstein
item.description:
Einstein brought AI to Salesforce customers well before generative AI became popular. Predictive features score leads and opportunities, forecast revenue, recommend next best actions, and flag at-risk accounts, using each company’s own CRM data. Einstein Discovery finds patterns and suggests what drives outcomes, and bots and analytics features extend the same ideas to service and marketing.

With generative AI, Einstein has expanded to write emails, summarize records and cases, and generate service replies, grounded in customer data and protected by the Einstein Trust Layer, which masks sensitive information and prevents customer data from being used to train outside models. The conversational assistant evolved into Agentforce, which builds autonomous agents on the same foundation, so Einstein now refers to a mix of older predictive features and the generative AI infrastructure.

item.title: SAP Ariba
item.description:
SAP Ariba helps large organizations buy what they need in an organized way. Procurement teams use it to find and evaluate suppliers, run sourcing events, manage contracts, process purchase orders and invoices, and monitor supplier risk. The Ariba Network connects buyers and suppliers electronically, so orders and invoices flow between systems without manual entry.

AI is being added to reduce manual work. SAP’s assistant, Joule, can help users search for information, draft sourcing documents, and answer questions about spend, and features analyze contracts, recommend suppliers, and flag unusual transactions. Integration with SAP’s ERP and other systems provides a connected view of purchasing, and spend analytics reveal savings opportunities.

item.title: Scale AI
item.description:
Scale AI built its business on a simple observation: AI models need huge amounts of well-labeled data, and quality control at scale is hard. It combines software with a large network of human contributors and experts to annotate images, video, text, and sensor data. Early customers included self-driving car developers, and the company grew by supplying training data to the biggest AI labs.

Today much of its work involves large language models. Scale provides human feedback data used in reinforcement learning, expert-written examples for fine-tuning, and evaluations that test models for accuracy and safety. Its tools help companies manage data pipelines, and a generative AI platform lets enterprises customize models on their own data. Public-sector work includes AI systems for defense and government agencies, and the company runs public leaderboards that rank models on hard tests.

item.title: Scinapse
item.description:
Scinapse is a search tool for scientific literature. It indexes a large body of scholarly papers across disciplines and ranks results with machine learning that considers relevance, citations, and recency. Users search by topic, title, or author, filter by year, journal, and field, and read abstracts with links to the publishers or open-access copies.

Features go beyond a basic list. Author pages show a researcher’s publications and citation profile, paper pages show who cited a work and related papers, and collections let you save papers to read later. Alerts notify you about new papers on a topic or from an author. The site was created by a Korean research technology company and is free to use, supported by its broader services for researchers.

item.title: SciSpace
item.description: SciSpace, formerly known as Typeset, is built around the problem of reading dense research. Upload a PDF or open a paper from its database, and an AI copilot lets you highlight a passage, a table, or an equation and ask for an explanation in simpler terms. You can also ask questions about the whole paper, request a summary, or get the key methods and results. It is helpful for students and researchers entering an unfamiliar field.

item.title: Semantic Scholar
item.description: Semantic Scholar is a research search engine built by the Allen Institute for AI, a nonprofit research organization. It covers hundreds of millions of academic papers across science, medicine, engineering, and the social sciences, and it is free. Unlike a plain keyword search, it uses language models to understand what papers are about and how they connect, which helps surface relevant work that does not use the exact words you typed.

item.title: Sembly AI
item.description:
Sembly joins your online meetings, records them, and produces a transcript with a structured summary. The summary highlights the main points, tasks, decisions, and risks mentioned, so teams can see what needs follow-up without rewatching. It also supports in-person meetings through its mobile app and uploads of audio files, and works in many languages.

Beyond single meetings, Sembly helps organize knowledge. Workspaces and meeting libraries let teams search past conversations and ask questions across them, and templates adjust the notes for different meeting types such as sales calls or interviews. Integrations push summaries and tasks into Slack, Notion, Asana, Jira, HubSpot, and other tools. Analytics track patterns like meeting time and topics.

item.title: SEMrush
item.description:
Semrush bundles many marketing tools in one subscription. Users research keywords, audit websites, track rankings, analyze backlinks, spy on competitors’ traffic and ads, and plan content, all from a shared dashboard. It is widely used by agencies and in-house teams.

AI features help with writing and analysis. A writing assistant drafts and optimizes content, AI tools summarize data and suggest actions, and newer products track how brands appear in AI-generated answers from chat assistants, a growing concern for search marketers. Reports and integrations suit client work.

item.title: SEMrush
item.description: Semrush is among the most widely used toolkits for search marketers. Its core is a big database of keywords and domains, so you can see which terms a competitor ranks for, how much traffic a page gets, who links to it, and where your own site stands. Keyword research, position tracking, site audits, and backlink analysis cover the regular work of search optimization. Separate tools handle paid search, content planning, local listings, and social media.

item.title: SimilarWeb
item.description:
Similarweb lets you look at the performance of sites you do not own. Enter a domain, and it shows estimated monthly visits, traffic sources such as search, social, and direct, top keywords, referring sites, audience demographics, and engagement metrics like time on site. Data comes from a mix of panels, partnerships, and public sources, modeled to produce estimates. This helps in benchmarking competitors and finding growth opportunities.

The platform covers more than websites. It tracks app usage and downloads, advertising, and market segments, and ranks sites within categories. Recent additions include tracking how brands and sites are cited and visited through AI chatbots, reflecting the way people increasingly use AI assistants instead of search. Investors use the data to spot trends in company performance before financial reports, and sales teams use it to find leads.

item.title: Sisense
item.description:
Sisense helps organizations analyze data and share insights. Analysts connect data sources, build models and dashboards, and users explore results in a browser. Its strength is embedding: software companies place Sisense charts and analytics inside their products for customers.

AI features include asking questions in plain language, forecasting, and automatic detection of unusual patterns, plus a generative assistant that builds dashboards. The platform works with cloud data warehouses and offers an API-first approach.

item.title: SocialBee
item.description:
SocialBee organizes posting by category, such as promotions, tips, and behind-the-scenes, so a profile keeps a deliberate mix rather than random posts. Evergreen content can be recycled automatically, and a calendar shows what is scheduled.

AI helps generate posts, captions, and images, and its Copilot suggests a strategy and content plan from a business description. Team features support approvals and client work, and analytics report performance.

SocialBee is paid, with plans by profiles. Alternatives include Buffer, Later, Publer, Hootsuite, and Metricool. SocialBee suits small businesses and agencies.

item.title: Softr
item.description:
Softr turns data into software. A user connects Airtable, Google Sheets, or its own database, and builds pages with blocks such as lists, forms, dashboards, and charts. Logins and permissions control which users see which records.

Typical products include client portals, directories, simple CRMs, and internal tools. The AI builder creates an app from a description, and workflows automate actions. Hosting and a custom domain are included.

Softr has a free plan and paid tiers by users and features. Complex logic is limited compared with full code. Alternatives include Glide, Pory, Stacker, Bubble, and Retool. Softr suits non-developers building apps on spreadsheets and databases.

item.title: Spotify for Podcasters
item.description:
Spotify for Podcasters grew from Anchor, an app that made podcasting free and easy. Creators can record from a phone or computer, upload episodes, and publish to Spotify, Apple Podcasts, and other directories from one place, with no hosting fees. Tools include simple editing, music and sound effects, and a way to bring in guests remotely.

The creator tools have expanded to include video podcasts, which Spotify has promoted heavily, along with analytics on audience size, demographics, and listening behavior. Monetization options include ad insertion, listener subscriptions, and partner programs for eligible shows. The brand has been folded into Spotify for Creators, which covers audio and video content creators on the platform.

item.title: Sprout Social
item.description:
Sprout Social is built for teams that manage social media as a function, not a side task. A calendar plans and schedules content across networks such as Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, X, and TikTok, and approval flows keep drafts under review before they go out. A smart inbox gathers messages, comments, and mentions from every channel into one stream that can be assigned, tagged, and replied to by a team.

Analytics are a major selling point. Reports show how posts perform, how audiences grow, and how competitors compare, and they can be exported or shared with clients and executives. Listening tools track brand mentions, topics, and sentiment across social and the web, which helps with crisis monitoring and market research. Influencer marketing and employee advocacy tools extend into related work. AI Assist helps write posts, change tone, and draft replies, and it can summarize sentiment from conversations.

item.title: Square
item.description:
Square is known for its card readers and registers. A small business accepts payments in person, online, or by invoice, tracks inventory, and manages staff and payroll from a single account. Hardware ranges from a simple reader to full countertop systems.

Additional services include appointments, loyalty programs, marketing, and small business loans based on sales. AI assistance writes item descriptions, generates insights from sales data, and answers business questions.

Square charges processing fees per transaction and sells hardware, with paid software tiers for advanced features. It has a free plan for basic use. Alternatives include Toast for restaurants, Clover, Shopify POS, Stripe Terminal, and SumUp. Square suits small retail and food businesses.

item.title: Stamped.io
item.description:
Stamped helps online stores build trust. After a purchase, it emails customers asking for reviews, collects star ratings with photos or videos, and displays them on product pages and in search results with structured data. Social proof improves conversion rates, and review requests can be automated and timed, with options to send coupons for leaving a review.

The platform also offers loyalty and referral programs. Customers earn points for purchases and actions, redeem rewards, and refer friends, which encourages repeat business. AI features summarize reviews into key themes, surface what customers love or dislike, and help merchants respond. Reports show review volume, ratings, and the effect on sales, and integrations connect with email, helpdesk, and ads tools.

item.title: Stampli
item.description:
Stampli keeps the conversation about an invoice attached to the invoice. When a bill arrives, teams discuss it in context, approvers sign off, and the payment goes out, with no hunting through email threads. It connects to accounting systems and does not require replacing them.

Billy the Bot reads invoices, suggests coding and approvals based on past behavior, and flags anomalies. Payment tools handle payments and cards, and the platform provides audit trails and reporting.

item.title: Supabase AI
item.description:
Supabase provides what an application needs behind the scenes. It gives developers a hosted Postgres database with auto-generated APIs, user authentication, file storage, real-time updates, and serverless edge functions, all manageable from a web dashboard. It’s often described as an open-source alternative to Firebase, with the advantage of using standard SQL and a portable database.

For AI, Supabase supports the pgvector extension, which stores embeddings in Postgres and enables similarity search, so developers can build semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation without a separate vector database. Edge functions can call language models, and an AI assistant in the dashboard helps write SQL and design schemas. It has become a popular backend for AI app builders such as Lovable and Bolt.

item.title: Surfer SEO
item.description: Surfer helps writers create content that matches what already ranks. You enter a keyword and it analyzes the top search results, then suggests the terms, headings, length, and structure those pages share. As you write in its editor, a content score updates, giving a quick sense of how well your page covers the topic. Writers and SEO teams use it to guide drafts and to update old posts that have dropped in rankings.

item.title: Tableau
item.description:
Tableau is known for making data exploration feel visual and quick. Analysts connect to databases, spreadsheets, and cloud data warehouses, then drag fields onto a canvas to build charts, maps, and dashboards without writing code. It handles large data volumes well, and its interactivity lets viewers filter, drill down, and compare in ways static reports cannot. It is widely used in finance, healthcare, retail, government, and education.

Salesforce owns Tableau and has built AI into it. Tableau Pulse sends personalized, plain-language insights about key metrics to the people who care about them, and flags unusual changes without anyone opening a dashboard. Tableau Agent helps users build visualizations and analyze data by chatting with the tool. Tableau Prep cleans and combines data, and the platform integrates with Salesforce data and its Data Cloud.

item.title: ThoughtSpot
item.description:
ThoughtSpot built its product around search. Instead of building reports by dragging fields, business users type a question such as sales by region last quarter, and ThoughtSpot generates the right chart from the connected data warehouse, with the ability to drill down and refine. This lowers the barrier for people who are not analysts and reduces the queue of requests for data teams.

Generative AI has expanded the approach. Spotter acts as an AI analyst that understands questions in conversation, runs analyses, explains results, and proposes follow-up questions, while agents can answer questions inside other tools. Liveboards combine charts into shareable dashboards that update from live data, and an embedded analytics offering lets companies put these capabilities in their own products.

item.title: Tipalti
item.description:
Tipalti automates accounts payable for growing companies. Suppliers and partners onboard through a portal that collects tax forms and payment details, invoices are captured and approved, and Tipalti pays them in the local currency and method across many countries.

Compliance is a main benefit: the platform handles tax documentation, sanctions screening, and reporting, which is hard for companies paying people worldwide. AI reads invoices, flags anomalies, and helps reconcile payments in accounting systems.

item.title: Toast
item.description:
Toast serves the restaurant industry. Servers take orders on handheld devices, kitchen displays route tickets, guests pay at the table or online, and managers track sales, labor, and inventory. Online ordering, delivery integrations, and loyalty programs are part of the ecosystem.

Data and AI support operations. Sales forecasts help schedule staff, menu analytics show what sells, and assistants help write menu descriptions and answer business questions. Payroll and team management tools extend the suite.

item.title: Undermind
item.description: Undermind is designed for the situation where a simple search leaves you wondering what you missed. You describe your research question in plain language, including constraints and nuance, and the agent runs a deep search: it queries multiple sources, reads abstracts and text, follows citations, and refines its search based on what it finds. After some minutes, it delivers a ranked list of relevant papers with explanations of why each matches.

item.title: Wolfram Alpha AI
item.description: Wolfram Alpha doesn’t search the web. It computes answers. Ask it to integrate a function, convert units, compare populations, or show the weather on a given date, and it uses curated data and algorithms, written in the Wolfram Language, to produce a result with steps, charts, and data. That makes it reliable for math, physics, chemistry, statistics, and factual queries with definite answers, which is where language models often make mistakes.

item.title: Wordsmith
item.description:
Wordsmith turns data into text. Users define templates and logic, connect a data source, and the platform writes a narrative for each record, such as a financial summary, a sports recap, or a personalized report. The output is consistent and can be produced in volume.

It predates today’s chat models. Rule-based natural language generation gives predictable text, which suits regulated reporting where exact control matters, while large language models offer flexibility and fluency but less predictability.

item.title: Workday
item.description:
Workday began as cloud HR software and expanded into financials. Large employers use it to keep employee records, run payroll and benefits, manage recruiting and performance, plan headcount and budgets, and close the books. Having HR and finance on one data model helps companies tie workforce decisions to costs.

AI shows up across the suite. It suggests candidates and skills matches, flags attrition risks, helps managers with planning, and drafts job descriptions and summaries. Workday has also introduced AI agents that take on tasks inside its apps, along with an agent management layer so that companies can control what those agents may do. It has bought AI companies to extend this, including some that build agent platforms.

item.title: Yodlee
item.description:
Yodlee lets financial apps pull in customers’ account data. A budgeting tool, lender, or wealth platform can use Yodlee’s APIs to link to thousands of financial institutions, retrieve balances and transactions, and keep them updated. That saves each company from building separate connections to every bank.

Beyond raw data, Yodlee enriches transactions. Machine learning cleans merchant names, assigns categories, and flags patterns, and analytics products use aggregated data to describe consumer spending trends. Account verification and income checks help lenders confirm information, and the company supports open banking rules in regions where they exist.

item.title: Yotpo
item.description:
Yotpo helps online stores build trust and repeat business. It collects reviews with photos, shows them on product pages and in search, and runs loyalty programs and referral offers. SMS and email tools extend marketing.

AI summarizes reviews into themes, flags issues, and drafts responses, and analytics tie content to conversion. Integrations cover Shopify, BigCommerce, and other platforms.

Yotpo has a free tier and paid plans that scale with orders. Alternatives include Okendo, Judge.me, Stamped.io, Klaviyo, and Trustpilot. Yotpo suits growing online stores.

item.title: Zeni
item.description:
Zeni provides outsourced finance for startups. Companies connect their bank accounts, and Zeni handles bookkeeping, accounts payable, tax, and CFO services, with a dashboard showing cash, burn, and runway in real time. Humans check the AI’s work.

The service replaces a part-time accountant or finance hire for early-stage companies. Monthly reports help founders and investors understand the business.

Zeni is a subscription service. Alternatives include Pilot, Bench, Puzzle, Digits, and a traditional accountant. Zeni suits startups wanting outsourced finance.

item.title: Zoho
item.description:
Zoho builds a wide range of business applications on its own platform.
