Companies can use Zoho CRM for sales, Books for accounting, Desk for support, Projects for work tracking, Mail for email, People for HR, and dozens of other apps, many of which integrate with one another. Zoho One bundles the whole suite for a single per-user price.

Zia is the AI layer. It predicts which leads are likely to convert, detects anomalies in data, drafts replies, and answers questions in natural language, and Zoho has added a generative assistant and agents that can act across apps. The company also supports the option of running models on its own infrastructure for customers who want data kept in their region.

item.title: Zotero
item.description:
Zotero saves references with a click. A browser connector captures a paper or web page along with its citation details and PDF, and the library organizes items in collections with tags and notes. Word and Google Docs plugins insert citations in thousands of styles.

Group libraries support collaboration, and the open ecosystem has plugins for annotation, syncing, and AI summaries and search. Because it is community driven and non-profit, users keep control over data.

item.title: Ashby
item.description:
Ashby brings together tools that recruiting teams often buy separately. The core is an applicant tracking system for jobs, candidates, and interview plans. Around it sit scheduling that coordinates interviewers automatically, a CRM for sourcing and nurturing talent, and an analytics layer that shows pipeline health, time to hire, and source effectiveness.

AI features handle repetitive work, such as summarizing candidates, drafting outreach, and taking notes in interviews. Structured scorecards and interview plans promote consistent evaluation, and reporting is built into the product rather than added on, which analytics-minded recruiting teams like.

item.title: Attio
item.description:
Attio starts from the idea that every company sells differently. Instead of fixed objects like leads and opportunities, teams build their own structures, such as customers, partners, or investors, and link them. The interface feels more like a spreadsheet and a database than a traditional CRM, so it is easier to reshape.

Data fills in with little typing. Attio connects to email and calendar to log interactions, enriches company and contact details, and shows the strength of relationships. AI features summarize accounts, answer questions about the pipeline, and fill in fields from conversations. Workflow automation moves records, sends notifications, and updates data.

item.title: Beehiiv
item.description:
Beehiiv is built for people who run newsletters as a business. Writers compose and send posts, manage subscriber lists, and publish a website for the archive. Growth tools include referral programs, recommendations between newsletters, and landing pages, which help build an audience without outside ads.

Monetization is a central feature. Creators can sell paid subscriptions, run ads through the Beehiiv ad network, add sponsors, and offer digital products. Analytics show opens, clicks, and which posts convert readers. An AI assistant helps with drafts, subject lines, and ideas, and automation handles welcome sequences.

item.title: Braze
item.description:
Braze helps brands talk to customers on the channels where they spend time. Marketers segment users by behavior, design journeys in a visual canvas, and send messages triggered by actions such as opening an app, abandoning a cart, or reaching a milestone. Real-time data means messages respond to what is happening now.

AI features improve targeting and creation. Predictive models estimate who might churn or buy, optimization chooses the best send time and channel for each person, and generative tools help write subject lines and copy. Analytics measure the effect of campaigns on retention and revenue.

item.title: Brex
item.description:
Brex built a corporate card and spend platform for startups and growing companies. Businesses issue cards to employees with set limits, and expenses are captured and matched automatically, with receipts collected through the app and policies enforced in real time. Finance teams get visibility into spending and can close their books faster than with manual expense reports.

The platform grew into a broader finance system. It includes bill payments, reimbursements, travel booking, banking features, and budgeting, with integrations to accounting software such as NetSuite and QuickBooks. AI agents handle tasks such as filling out expense reports, checking receipts for policy violations, and answering finance questions, aiming to reduce time spent on back-office work.

item.title: Cleanlab
item.description:
Cleanlab starts from the idea that model quality depends on data quality. Real datasets contain mistakes: images with wrong labels, duplicated examples, and outliers. Cleanlab’s open-source library uses statistical methods and model predictions to find the examples most likely to be wrong, so a team can correct them instead of reviewing everything.

The commercial platform, Cleanlab Studio, extends this with a no-code interface for cleaning and improving datasets and training models on the result. The company has also moved into reliability for generative AI, offering tools to score the trustworthiness of language model outputs and catch hallucinations in production systems.

item.title: CleverTap
item.description:
CleverTap serves brands with mobile apps and large user bases. It collects behavioral data such as app opens, purchases, and feature use, builds segments, and lets marketers send push notifications, email, SMS, WhatsApp, and in-app messages. Journeys can be designed visually so that actions trigger the next message.

AI is used for prediction and optimization. Models estimate which users are likely to churn or convert, choose the best time and channel for each message, and recommend products. A proprietary database designed for large volumes of event data keeps analysis fast, and analytics show retention, funnels, and campaign results.

item.title: CSM AI
item.description:
CSM turns simple inputs into 3D assets. A user uploads a picture, types a description, or draws a sketch, and the system produces a 3D model with textures that can be exported to common formats. It supports game developers, designers, and creators who need assets quickly.

Beyond single objects, it offers tools for character creation and animation preparation, and an API lets developers build 3D generation into their own apps. The output is often a starting point that artists clean up, since generated meshes can have topology problems that matter for animation and games.

item.title: Flatiron Health
item.description:
Flatiron Health works in cancer care. Its electronic health record, OncoEMR, is used by many community oncology practices, and the data from those practices, once de-identified and curated, form a large real-world dataset. Researchers use it to study how treatments work outside clinical trials.

The company uses machine learning and human abstraction to turn unstructured notes into research-ready data. Biopharma companies use these datasets to understand patient populations, design trials, and support regulatory submissions. Products for clinics include tools for clinical workflows, billing, and trial matching.

item.title: Gem
item.description:
Gem helps recruiting teams build pipelines. Recruiters search for candidates across LinkedIn and other sources, add them to talent pools, and send sequences of personalized outreach. A candidate CRM tracks every interaction, so when a role opens, the team can reach people they have already engaged.

Analytics show how sourcing channels perform, how long hiring takes, and where candidates drop out. AI features help with search, writing outreach, and identifying candidates who may be open to new roles. An applicant tracking system component extends the suite for teams that want everything in one place.

item.title: Ghost
item.description:
Ghost is a publishing tool focused on independent media. It provides a clean editor, a website with themes, email newsletters, and a membership system that lets readers subscribe for free or pay. Because it is open source, publishers can host it themselves or use Ghost’s managed service.

Business features are built in. Payments run through Stripe, so publishers keep most of the revenue, and analytics show how posts convert readers into members. The platform supports multiple tiers, comments, and integrations with other tools. A nonprofit organization develops it, which differs from venture-backed rivals.

item.title: Iconosquare
item.description:
Iconosquare started as an Instagram analytics tool and expanded to other networks. Social teams connect accounts and see how posts perform, when audiences are active, and how growth compares with competitors. Reports can be exported for clients, which makes it popular with agencies.

Scheduling and planning tools let teams build a content calendar and publish across networks. AI features suggest captions and hashtags, and a listening module monitors mentions and comments. The focus is on analysis that guides what to post, more than on broad community management.

item.title: Latte Social
item.description:
Latte Social covers the basics of content planning. Users connect accounts, ask the AI for post ideas and captions tuned to a brand’s voice, schedule content on a calendar, and publish to several networks. The tool aims to keep a steady posting schedule without constant effort.

For small teams and individual creators, that combination of drafting and scheduling reduces time spent on routine social tasks. AI-generated posts are a starting point and tend to be generic without personal details and specific examples.

item.title: Loomly
item.description:
Loomly supports the planning side of social media. Teams build a content calendar, get post ideas from trends and prompts, draft posts with images and links, and route them through an approval workflow before publishing. A brand asset library keeps logos and images handy.

The platform previews how a post will look on each network and schedules publishing. Analytics show performance, and ad management features support boosted posts. AI assists with captions and ideas.

item.title: Madgicx
item.description:
Madgicx is built for performance marketers and e-commerce brands running paid social. It connects to ad accounts and analyzes campaigns, then recommends or applies changes such as shifting budget toward better-performing ad sets, pausing losers, or testing new audiences. Automation rules run these changes continuously.

Creative tools help with the content side. The platform analyzes which creatives perform best and helps generate variations, and reporting dashboards combine data from ads and online stores into one view. Audience tools find lookalike segments and retargeting groups.

item.title: Mercury
item.description: Mercury provides online banking designed for startups. A founder can open a business account in minutes, get checking and savings, send and receive wires and ACH transfers, issue virtual and physical debit and credit cards, and pay bills, all in a clean web and mobile interface. Mercury is a financial technology company, not a bank itself, and works with partner banks to hold deposits and provide FDIC insurance through sweep arrangements.

item.title: Monarch Money
item.description:
Monarch Money brings accounts into one dashboard. Users link banks, cards, loans, and investments, and the app tracks spending, net worth, and recurring bills. Budgets can follow a flexible or category-based model, and goals help save toward targets.

Couples and families can share views and manage budgets together while keeping some accounts private. AI categorizes transactions, spots subscriptions, and gives summaries and insights, and an assistant answers questions about finances. Reports show trends over time.

item.title: Oliv AI
item.description:
Oliv AI assists sellers before, during, and after calls. Before a meeting, it gathers context on the account and contacts and drafts a briefing. During the call, it records and transcribes. Afterward, it writes notes, updates the CRM, and drafts follow-up emails.

For managers, it scores deals against frameworks such as MEDDIC and highlights risks and gaps, which supports coaching and forecasting. The product presents these functions as agents that take over routine sales admin.

item.title: Pallyy
item.description:
Pallyy keeps social management simple and affordable. Users connect accounts, plan posts on a visual calendar, and publish to several networks. A first-comment feature, link-in-bio pages, and a media library support common creator workflows, and a unified inbox collects comments and messages.

Analytics show growth and engagement, and client-friendly reports help agencies prove results. Collaboration tools let clients approve content before it goes live. AI features suggest captions, hashtags, and ideas to speed up planning.

item.title: Phenom
item.description:
Phenom helps employers attract and manage talent. Its career sites show candidates jobs and content tailored to their interests, a recruiting CRM nurtures talent pools, and tools handle scheduling, chat, and applications. The same platform supports employees through internal job matching and career paths.

AI infers skills from resumes and profiles to match people with roles, recommend jobs, and surface candidates already in the system. Analytics show the hiring funnel and diversity data. The company sells to large enterprises.

item.title: Publer
item.description:
Publer provides the essentials of social media planning at a modest price. Users connect accounts, build a calendar, schedule posts and recurring content, and see analytics on performance. Bulk scheduling and a library of media help manage volume.

Features include collaboration and approvals, link in bio pages, and a social inbox. The AI assistant writes captions, suggests hashtags, and repurposes content, and tools recycle evergreen posts.

Publer has a free plan with limits and paid tiers by social accounts. Alternatives include Buffer, Later, Metricool, Hootsuite, and Pallyy. Publer suits creators and small teams who want an affordable scheduler.

item.title: Quantilope
item.description:
Quantilope aims to let research teams run advanced studies without waiting weeks on an agency. Researchers pick from automated methods, such as concept tests, segmentation, pricing studies, and brand tracking, set up the survey, and field it to respondents from a panel. Analysis and charts are generated as data comes in.

The platform’s AI helps design studies, suggests suitable methods, writes summaries of findings, and answers questions about the data. Because methodologies are built in, non-specialists can run studies that would normally need a statistician.

item.title: Remesh
item.description:
Remesh scales the focus group. A moderator poses questions to hundreds of participants at once, and people respond in their own words and then rate each other’s answers, so the group quickly reveals where opinions agree and differ. Responses are analyzed as they arrive.

AI clusters comments into themes, summarizes sentiment, and highlights segments by demographic. Researchers use it for message testing, employee listening, public policy input, and product research. A single session can produce depth and breadth that would take many interviews.

item.title: SeekOut
item.description:
SeekOut builds a searchable database of professionals from public profiles and sources. Recruiters filter by skills, experience, and background, find candidates for roles like engineers and scientists, and reach out with outreach sequences.

AI helps match candidates to jobs and understand skill sets, and analytics show talent pools in a region or company. Diversity filters support recruiting programs, subject to legal rules on how they are used. Products extend to internal talent management for employers.

item.title: Trullion
item.description:
Trullion tackles accounting standards that require reading contracts. For leases and revenue contracts, finance teams must pull terms such as payments, dates, and options into calculations. Trullion’s AI reads documents, extracts the data, and generates the schedules and journal entries.

Each figure links back to its source in the document, which helps auditors verify. The platform integrates with accounting systems and handles changes such as lease modifications. It is used by finance teams and audit firms.

item.title: Vic.ai
item.description:
Vic.ai reads invoices and processes them with little manual input. It extracts data, suggests coding to the correct accounts, routes approvals, and flags unusual items, learning from how accountants correct it. The aim is touchless processing for routine invoices.

It integrates with ERP systems such as NetSuite, SAP, and Microsoft Dynamics, and offers payment and analytics features. Accounting firms and mid-sized to large finance teams use it to cut manual work.

item.title: Vista Social
item.description:
Vista Social covers social publishing end to end. Teams connect profiles, plan a calendar, schedule content, and respond to comments and messages in one inbox. Approval workflows suit agencies working with clients, and reports summarize performance.

The platform includes reputation management, with review monitoring, and tools for tracking competitors. The AI assistant writes captions, suggests hashtags, and repurposes content. It supports newer networks quickly, which agencies value.

Vista Social has a free plan and paid tiers by profiles and users. Alternatives include Hootsuite, Sprout Social, Buffer, Later, and Agorapulse. Vista Social suits agencies and brands managing many accounts.

item.title: AI Aware
item.description:
AI Aware presents itself as a tool for checking whether content was written or generated by AI. Users upload a document or paste text, and the service returns an estimate of how likely it is to be machine-generated, along with detail on which parts raised the score. The idea is to give educators, publishers, and businesses a quick way to screen material.

Detection of AI-generated content is a difficult problem. Detectors rely on statistical patterns that can also appear in human writing, especially in formal or non-native text, and they can be fooled by editing or paraphrasing. For that reason, any score should be treated as a hint that calls for further review rather than as proof.

item.title: BlogSEO
item.description:
BlogSEO aims to automate the path from keyword to published post. A user enters a topic or website, the tool finds relevant keywords, creates an outline based on what ranks, and drafts an article. Some workflows can schedule and publish posts directly to a content management system.

For small businesses without a writer, that can mean a steady flow of blog content. The risk is that generic, unedited AI articles rarely rank well and can weaken a site’s credibility. Search engines favor original, helpful pages, so the strongest use is to draft quickly and then add real expertise, examples, and fact-checking.

item.title: ChatPDF
item.description: ChatPDF is a simple tool for talking to a document. You upload a PDF or paste a link, and it reads the file and lets you ask for a summary, a definition, or a specific fact. Each answer includes references to the pages it came from, so you can check the passage yourself. Students use it to understand dense papers, professionals use it for contracts and reports, and people use it to find the right section of a long manual without scrolling.

item.title: Clearscope
item.description: Clearscope helps writers produce content that is complete enough to rank. You enter a keyword, and it analyzes the top results to show the terms, topics, and questions that strong pages tend to include. As you draft in its editor, a grade updates, so you can see whether the page covers what searchers expect. Plugins for Google Docs, Word, and WordPress let writers work in familiar tools instead of switching to a separate app.

item.title: Competitor Analyzer
item.description:
Competitor Analyzer helps small teams keep an eye on the market without a full-time analyst. You enter your competitors, and the tool watches their websites, social accounts, content, and in some cases pricing, then summarizes what changed in a weekly digest. The aim is to save the time spent checking sites by hand.

Typical uses include spotting a rival’s new feature or campaign, tracking pricing changes, and gathering material for positioning. AI summaries make the digests quick to read and highlight notable changes. The tool is positioned as simpler and cheaper than enterprise competitive intelligence platforms.

item.title: Connected Papers
item.description: Connected Papers helps you get oriented in a research area. You enter a paper title, DOI, or link, and it produces a graph where each node is a paper and closer nodes are more similar. Similarity comes from co-citation and bibliographic coupling, meaning papers that cite similar sources or are cited together, rather than from keywords. Node size and color show citation count and year, which lets you see influential and recent work at a glance.

item.title: Cresh
item.description:
Cresh is built for early-stage business research. A user describes an idea or market, and several AI agents search sources, gather information, and assemble a report covering competitors, market size, customer needs, and risks. The aim is a fast first pass that would otherwise require manual searching.

Founders use it to test ideas before investing time, and analysts use it to build starting briefs. Reports from AI research tools can contain errors and unsupported claims, so figures and sources should be checked before decisions or investor materials rely on them.

item.title: Evalyze
item.description:
Evalyze aims to make fundraising more systematic. A founder uploads a pitch deck, and the tool reviews it for clarity, story, and typical investor concerns, then suggests improvements. It also helps identify investors whose focus matches the company’s stage and sector.

For first-time founders, structured feedback is useful because many lack access to experienced advisors. Matching tools can narrow a long list of investors to those most likely to be interested, which saves time on outreach.

item.title: Fabricate
item.description:
Fabricate belongs to the group of prompt-to-app tools. A user describes the application, and the platform generates the interface, server logic, and data storage, then deploys it so it can be used right away. The user keeps refining by asking for changes in chat.

It is meant for prototypes, internal tools, and simple products. Getting from idea to something usable in minutes helps founders test concepts. Generated applications need testing, and authentication, payments, and security deserve a careful look before launch with real users.

item.title: GoAI
item.description:
GoAI aims to give individual investors some of the research help professionals have. A user searches a company or asks a question, and the tool pulls financial data, summarizes earnings calls and filings, and highlights notable insider trades. Answers are written in plain language to be readable for non-experts.

Such tools save time reading long documents, but they do not predict the market. AI summaries can contain errors, so important figures should be checked against filings. Past results do not guarantee future performance, and nothing a tool generates should be treated as a recommendation.

item.title: Hedy AI
item.description:
Hedy AI takes a different role from notetakers that summarize afterward. It listens during a call or conversation and shows prompts in the moment: a suggested answer, a question to ask, or a reminder of context. The goal is to help the user perform better while the conversation is happening.

After the meeting, it produces transcripts and summaries and can store notes for future sessions. People use it for sales calls, interviews, negotiations, and learning situations. It can run alongside video calls or in person on a phone or computer.

item.title: Humata
item.description: Humata lets people converse with documents. After you upload a file, it reads the content and answers questions about it: asking for a summary, a specific figure, a comparison between sections, or an explanation of a clause. Each answer includes a citation that links to the passage in the source, which makes it easy to verify. It works with long files that would take a long time to scan manually, such as contracts, research papers, and financial reports.

item.title: Instantly
item.description:
Instantly is built for outbound email at scale. You connect as many sending accounts as you like, and the platform rotates them to spread volume, which helps keep each account within safe sending limits. An automated warm-up network exchanges emails between accounts to build sender reputation, and tools check deliverability so campaigns are more likely to reach the inbox. Sequences handle follow-ups and stop when someone replies.

AI and data features add to the core sender. A lead database lets users find prospects by role, industry, and location, AI helps write and personalize email copy, and a unified inbox collects replies from all accounts in one place. Analytics show opens, replies, and bounces, and integrations connect with CRMs and automation tools. Agencies, sales teams, and lead generation businesses are the main users.

item.title: Iris.ai
item.description: Iris.ai aims to reduce the time scientists spend finding and reading relevant papers. Instead of keyword searches, a researcher can input a problem description or an abstract, and the system finds related papers by meaning. It then helps explore the results with a visual map of topics, filters based on content, and tools that extract data and summarize findings across many documents. Research teams use it to scan a field, check for prior work, and decide where to focus.

item.title: Julius AI
item.description: Julius lets people explore data by asking questions. After uploading a CSV or Excel file, or connecting to a database or Google Sheets, you can ask for things like the average sales by region, a trend over time, or a correlation between two columns. Julius writes and runs code behind the scenes, then shows the result as a chart, a table, or a written explanation, and you can view the code to check what it did.

item.title: Jupid
item.description:
Jupid is accounting help for sole proprietors. Users link their bank accounts and cards, and the app sorts each transaction into the categories used on Schedule C, which is the tax form for self-employment income. It flags business expenses, helps separate personal spending, and keeps a running view of profit.

The tool estimates quarterly taxes and highlights deductions that people often miss, which reduces the scramble at tax time. Reports can be exported to share with an accountant or to use when filing. AI handles the sorting and learns from corrections.

item.title: MarketAlerts.ai
item.description:
MarketAlerts.ai watches the market on behalf of its users. Investors list their holdings, and the service monitors news, filings, price moves, and other events, sending alerts when something relevant happens and summarizing why it might matter. Some alerts include AI-generated signals about possible actions.

Such tools save time for people who cannot follow the market all day, but they carry risks. AI-generated trade signals are not reliable predictions, markets are unpredictable, and acting on automated signals can lose money. Nothing here is financial advice.

item.title: Obviously AI
item.description:
Obviously AI was built to make machine learning accessible to business users. You upload a CSV or connect a data source, choose the thing you want to predict, such as customer churn, sales, or lead conversion, and the platform tests multiple algorithms, picks the best one, and shows the results in plain language. It highlights which columns most influence the prediction and lets you try what-if scenarios.

Predictions can be exported or sent to other tools, and the platform offers dashboards for sharing insights with teammates. It positions itself for marketing, sales, finance, and operations analysts who have data but no data scientists, and for consultants who need quick models for clients.

item.title: Page Pulse
item.description:
Page Pulse aims to make analytics approachable. A site owner adds a snippet and sees visitors, popular pages, sources, and conversions in a clear dashboard, without needing to learn a complex reporting interface. The focus is on answers to basic questions about what is working.

Typical users are small businesses, bloggers, and agencies that report to clients and want simple summaries. Some AI features explain trends in plain language and suggest improvements.

item.title: Pounce
item.description:
Pounce helps with timely engagement. It monitors social platforms for topics and conversations related to a brand or niche, flags those gaining traction, and suggests ways to participate, such as posting a response or creating content.

Social media managers use it to catch trends early, when joining a conversation can earn reach. Faster detection and suggested angles shorten the path from trend to post.

Independent information is limited. Brands should be careful about jumping on trends, as tone-deaf posts cause harm. Pounce has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Brandwatch, Sprout Social listening, Exploding Topics, BuzzSumo, and Google Trends. Pounce suits social managers who want trend alerts.

item.title: Predis.ai
item.description: Predis.ai aims to make social content creation quick for small businesses and creators. You enter a prompt or paste a link to your product page or website, choose a format such as a single image, carousel, or short video, and the tool generates a post with a caption, hashtags, and a branded design. Editing tools let you change the text, images, and layout, and apply your brand colors and logo.

item.title: Ramp
item.description:
Ramp issues corporate cards and wraps them in software for controlling spending. Companies give employees physical and virtual cards with limits and rules, and receipts are captured and matched automatically through the app. Finance teams see spending in real time and avoid chasing employees for expense reports. Ramp is known for fast growth among startups and mid-sized businesses.

The product has widened into a finance operating system. Bill pay handles vendor invoices, procurement tools manage purchase requests and approvals, and accounting automation categorizes transactions and syncs with systems such as NetSuite, QuickBooks, and Xero. AI agents review expenses against policy, suggest ways to cut costs from vendor spending data, and handle routine tasks such as coding transactions and preparing month-end close.

item.title: Scite
item.description: Scite changes how citation counts are read. A paper with many citations may be well supported or heavily disputed, and a raw count does not tell you which. Scite analyzes the text around each citation and labels it as supporting, contrasting, or mentioning, with a snippet of the citing sentence, so you can see how others have actually used a finding. It helps researchers judge reliability and spot controversial claims.

item.title: SEOJuice
item.description:
SEOJuice focuses on one SEO chore. Internal links help search engines understand a site and pass authority between pages, but adding them by hand across hundreds of articles is tedious. SEOJuice scans a site’s content, finds natural places to link related pages, and inserts the links automatically or for approval.

It installs through a script or plugin and keeps links updated as content grows. Additional tools include basic audits and content suggestions. It appeals to publishers and small businesses that lack time for manual optimization.

item.title: Taplio
item.description:
Taplio focuses on LinkedIn, where personal branding and B2B outreach happen. Users can generate post ideas and drafts in their own voice, find high-performing posts for inspiration, schedule content, and use carousels and templates. The AI learns from successful posts and tries to match your tone, saving time for busy founders, consultants, and sales professionals.

It includes tools beyond writing. Analytics show which posts and topics resonate and how followers grow, an engagement feature suggests relevant posts to comment on, and a lead database helps find and track potential customers. Team plans allow agencies and ghostwriters to manage multiple accounts.

item.title: The SEO Agent
item.description:
The SEO Agent automates the content workflow. A user enters a site or topic, and the tool finds keywords, plans articles, and writes drafts optimized for search, with options to publish to a content management system.

It targets small sites and marketers who need regular content. The risk with automated SEO articles is quality: generic or inaccurate content rarely ranks well and can hurt a site’s credibility, so editing and original insight matter.

item.title: Typefully
item.description:
Typefully started as a better way to write threads on X. The editor is clean and focused, with automatic thread splitting, a preview of how the post will look, and collaboration so someone else can review drafts. Posts can be scheduled, queued, and cross-posted to several networks, so one piece of writing can reach audiences on different platforms.

Analytics and growth features help creators learn what works. Dashboards show impressions, engagement, and follower trends, and tools help plan content, track ideas, and reuse past posts. AI features suggest rewrites, hooks, and alternatives, and can adjust tone, though the tool emphasizes the writer’s voice.

item.title: Wordrific
item.description:
Wordrific aims to simplify content production for marketing teams. A user starts with a topic or keyword, the tool researches what ranks, builds a brief, and drafts an article that follows it. The pieces of the workflow sit in one product instead of several.

B2B content has to be accurate and credible, and AI drafts need expert review and original insight to be useful. Scale without quality does not help rankings.
